The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

Two practices meet in the idea of a conversation that asks, and a third stands behind its last register.

The first is slot filling. A dialogue framework asks the user for the missing pieces of a form until the form is full. The frameworks of the field understand free text with trained models, speak on many channels and ship connectors, and they ask the designer to write intents and flows in their own language. They take the user's reply as the answer and act on it.

The second is vibe coding, a name put into circulation in 2025: the human prompts, the model produces, the human keeps what runs.

The third is programming by example. Spreadsheets fill a column from two examples you typed. Research calls it inductive synthesis, and the model era made the example the way one steers a model. (General knowledge, not a study of the record; the dates are to be checked before print.)

2. The first principle

A reply may come in any of five forms. Whatever the form, it is only a candidate, and the world's rules decide whether it becomes knowledge.

The design document says it in one sentence I keep: expression is free, admission is governed. [AUTHOR: The record holds this sentence as "captured from the author's directive" on 13 July 2026, and no sentence of yours on why these five registers and not four or six, nor on the moment you set wise coding against vibe coding. Is there an earlier sentence or memory the chapter should open on?]

3. The Softanza form

Chapter 17 showed a conversation asking, and refusing to conclude while a gap is open. This chapter is about the answer. The five registers are five forms a reply can take: an option picked by its number, a data structure, a formula, a sentence, and examples. I will show you each, and I will tell you the ones that do not run.

The first register: an option. When the world already knows values, the question offers them as numbers, and a number picks one.

Haro
oKB = new stzKnowledgeGraph("pizzeria")
oKB.Know("pizza1", "dish").Know("pizza2", "dish").Know("pizza3", "dish").Know("pizza4", "dish")
oKB.AddConversationQ("frame").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "topping"))
oKB.AskIn("frame")
oKB.ReplyIn("frame", "cheese")
oKB.AskIn("frame")
oKB.ReplyIn("frame", "olives")
? oKB.AskIn("frame")
#--> Which 'topping' does 'pizza3' have? (1) cheese  (2) olives -- or answer freely.  (why: every dish needs 'topping')
? @@(oKB.ReplyIn("frame", 2)[:admitted])
#--> [ "olives" ]

ran: printed what this block promises

A number nobody offered is refused, with its reason. The refusal never guesses a value, it reaches a person as a checkpoint, and the goal stays open:

Haro
? oKB.AskIn("frame")
#--> Which 'topping' does 'pizza4' have? (1) cheese  (2) olives -- or answer freely.  (why: every dish needs 'topping')
aV = oKB.ReplyIn("frame", 99)
? @@(aV[:admitted])
#--> [ ]
? @@(aV[:refused])
#--> [ [ "(99)", "no such option" ] ]
? oKB.ConversationQ("frame").Checkpoints()[1][:why]
#--> no option (99) was offered -- 2 option(s) on the table
? aV[:goalState]
#--> pursuing

ran: printed what this block promises

Look at what the refusal says: a reason, and a count of the options on the table. It does not list them, and the next question offers the same options again. That matters for section 7.

The question is data before it is text. It carries a force, which is what while the world knows nothing and which once it knows a value, and the options. Any medium can render it:

Haro
oKF = new stzKnowledgeGraph("pizzeria2")
oKF.Know("p1", "dish").Know("p2", "dish")
oKF.AddConversationQ("f").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "topping"))
? oKF.AskInXT("f")[:force]
#--> what
oKF.ReplyIn("f", "cheese")
aQ = oKF.AskInXT("f")
? aQ[:force]
#--> which
? @@(aQ[:options])
#--> [ "cheese" ]

ran: printed what this block promises

The second register: a data structure. A list of values is taken as the values, and each one goes through the same door.

Haro
oKD = new stzKnowledgeGraph("desserts")
oKD.Know("tiramisu", "dish")
oKD.AddConversationQ("setup").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "contains"))
oKD.AskIn("setup")
aV = oKD.ReplyIn("setup", [ "mascarpone", "espresso" ])
? @@(aV[:admitted])
#--> [ "mascarpone", "espresso" ]
? aV[:goalState]
#--> fulfilled

ran: printed what this block promises

The fourth register: a sentence. (I skip the third for a moment, because it is one of the two that do not run.) A phrase of the form "X and Y" or "X, Y" is read as two values, each one judged. The conversation keeps a transcript in which every admission is narrated and the fulfilment of the goal is recorded:

Haro
oKM = new stzKnowledgeGraph("menu")
oKM.Know("margherita", "dish")
oKM.AddConversationQ("setup").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "contains"))
oKM.AskIn("setup")
oKM.ReplyIn("setup", "tomato-sauce and mozzarella")
? oKM.ConversationQ("setup").Transcript()
#--> SOFTANZA: Goal adopted -- this conversation is now accountable for it.
#--> SOFTANZA: What does 'margherita' have for 'contains'?  (why: every dish needs 'contains')
#--> YOU:      tomato-sauce and mozzarella
#-->   -> admitted: 'margherita' contains 'tomato-sauce'
#-->   -> admitted: 'margherita' contains 'mozzarella'
#--> SOFTANZA: Goal fulfilled: every required slot is filled in 'menu'

ran: printed what this block promises

"Natural" here means a splitter on commas and on the English word "and". The natural layer of the library, which I will use in a moment, is not called by the conversation.

When a reply carries several values, and the world allows one. A relation declared unique takes the first value and refuses the others, each with the law's reason. The refusal reaches a person:

Haro
oKS = new stzKnowledgeGraph("staffing")
oKS.AddConversationQ("s").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireOne("kitchen3", "led-by"))
oKS.ConstrainRelation("led-by", :Unique)
oKS.AskIn("s")
aV = oKS.ReplyIn("s", "mario and giovanni")
? @@(aV[:admitted])
#--> [ "mario" ]
? @@(aV[:refused])
#--> [ [ "giovanni", "'kitchen3' already bears 'led-by' (to 'mario'); the relation is :Unique" ] ]
? len(oKS.ConversationQ("s").Checkpoints())
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

Be careful what you read in this. The choice between Mario and Giovanni was made by order. It was not made by a person. The design promises something else, and section 7 says what.

The third register, the formula. A formula typed as a reply is not evaluated. It is taken for a value:

Haro
oKP = new stzKnowledgeGraph("shop")
oKP.Know("tea", "product")
oKP.AddConversationQ("price").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("product", "price"))
oKP.AskIn("price")
? @@(oKP.ReplyIn("price", "=12*3")[:admitted])
#--> [ "=12*3" ]
? oKP.Query([ "tea", "price", "?o" ])[1]
#--> =12*3

ran: printed what this block promises

The price of the tea is now the text "=12*3". I found this out by running it, and the code is silent about a formula register. The record calls it the next work, filed and not routed.

The fifth register, examples. When examples are offered as pairs, they are neither admitted nor refused. The goal stays open, and no checkpoint is written. The agent that would read them is on the roster, and reserved:

Haro
oKX = new stzKnowledgeGraph("phones")
oKX.Know("contact1", "contact")
oKX.AddConversationQ("fmt").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("contact", "number-pattern"))
oKX.AskIn("fmt")
aV = oKX.ReplyIn("fmt", [ [ "+216-21-298-374", "valid" ], [ "+33-6-12-34-56-78", "valid" ] ])
? @@(aV[:admitted])
#--> [ ]
? @@(aV[:refused])
#--> [ ]
? aV[:goalState]
#--> pursuing
? len(oKX.ConversationQ("fmt").Checkpoints())
#--> 0
try
	StzOwnAgent("induction")
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> Softanza's own agent 'induction' is RESERVED, not wired yet -- refusing rather than returning a stub (LAW 3). See StzOwnAgents().

ran: printed what this block promises

This is not the refusal the protocol describes. It is silence, and silence is the worse answer: the reader who offered the examples is not told they were not understood. I found a second form of the same fault. The same examples typed as one string, joined by a comma, are split and admitted as two literal values, and the goal reads fulfilled. The examples became the knowledge. Nothing was inferred.

So three of the five registers are wired, one of them in its simplest form, a splitter. Two are not. I would rather you meet that here than on a page of mine that said five.

What happens to a refusal

A refusal waits for a person, with its context. A lifetime can be set so that a stale one leaves the live list without being deleted:

Haro
oKT = new stzKnowledgeGraph("ttl")
oKT.AddConversationQ("t").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireOne("kitchen", "led-by"))
oKT.AskIn("t")
oKT.ReplyIn("t", 7)
? len(oKT.ConversationQ("t").Checkpoints())
#--> 1
oKT.ConversationQ("t").SetCheckpointTTL(1)
oKT.AskIn("t")
oKT.AskIn("t")
? len(oKT.ConversationQ("t").Checkpoints())
#--> 0
? len(oKT.ConversationQ("t").AllCheckpoints())
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

Nothing is deleted. Expiry is about what still needs a person, and the audit record keeps all of it. Every call here is chained from ConversationQ, because a held copy would silently do nothing: the guard's comment explains it.

A conversation is accountable for one goal, and it ends by fulfilling the goal or by revoking it on the record. A revoked conversation asks nothing and cannot conclude:

Haro
oKG = new stzKnowledgeGraph("lifecycle")
oKG.Know("d1", "dish").Know("d2", "dish")
oKG.AddConversationQ("s1").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "sauce"))
oKG.AddConversationQ("s2").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "garnish"))
? oKG.ConversationQ("s1").GoalState()
#--> pursuing
oKG.AskIn("s1")
oKG.ReplyIn("s1", "pesto")
oKG.AskIn("s1")
oKG.ReplyIn("s1", "pesto")
? oKG.ConversationQ("s1").GoalState()
#--> fulfilled
? oKG.ConversationQ("s1").GoalWhy()
#--> every required slot is filled in 'lifecycle'
oKG.AskIn("s2")
oKG.ConversationQ("s2").RevokeGoal("out of scope tonight")
? oKG.ConversationQ("s2").GoalState()
#--> revoked
? oKG.ConversationQ("s2").GoalWhy()
#--> out of scope tonight
? len(oKG.OpenConversations())
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

Programmatic by default: the conversation with no one in it

Chapter 17's law says conversations happen in code first. Here is the conversation with no person and no model. An agent of the library asks, an answer source (a plain function) replies, and every reply passes the same door. Where the source has no answer, the agent stops and leaves the gap for a person. It does not invent:

Haro
oKW = new stzKnowledgeGraph("menu")
oKW.Know("margherita", "dish").Know("tiramisu", "dish")
answers = [ [ "margherita", "tomato-sauce" ], [ "tiramisu", "mascarpone" ] ]
aR = StzOwnAgent("wise-coder").PursueGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "contains"), oKW, func subj, rel {
	for a in answers
		if a[1] = subj
			return a[2]
		ok
	next
	return ""
})
? aR[:filled]
#--> 1
? aR[:asked]
#--> 2
? aR[:why]
#--> goal filled in 2 question(s), governed admission throughout
oKV = new stzKnowledgeGraph("desserts")
oKV.Know("panna-cotta", "dish")
aR2 = StzOwnAgent("wise-coder").PursueGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "contains"), oKV, func subj, rel { return "" })
? aR2[:filled]
#--> 0
? aR2[:why]
#--> stopped: no answer for 'panna-cotta' / 'contains' -- gap left for a human

ran: printed what this block promises

Of the library's five own agents, this is the one that is wired. The other four are reserved, and asking for one raises. It is never a stub.

In Arabic, and in Hausa

Chapters 2 and 11 showed the natural layer in Hausa. Here is what the conversation can and cannot do with languages, said in three blocks, because the three are different.

First, the data. Names, values and lists in Arabic script pass the gate exactly as Latin ones do. The words around them, the frame of the question, stay English:

Haro
oKA = new stzKnowledgeGraph("مطعم")
oKA.Know("بيتزا", "dish")
oKA.AddConversationQ("c").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "contains"))
? oKA.AskIn("c")
#--> What does 'بيتزا' have for 'contains'?  (why: every dish needs 'contains')
aV = oKA.ReplyIn("c", [ "جبن", "طماطم" ])
? @@(aV[:admitted])
#--> [ "جبن", "طماطم" ]
? aV[:goalState]
#--> fulfilled

ran: printed what this block promises

Second, the candidate. A Hausa sentence can produce a value in the natural layer, and the value, sent as a reply, goes through the same door. The two steps are the caller's: the conversation does not call the natural layer itself. This is the principle of the chapter in a small space, since the expression is free and the admission is governed. The graph folds the case of the value, so the capitals become 'jibini':

Haro
oKH = new stzKnowledgeGraph("menu")
oKH.Know("pizza", "dish")
oKH.AddConversationQ("c").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireEach("dish", "contains"))
oKH.AskIn("c")
cCandidate = NaturallyIn("ha", "Yi rubutu dauke 'jibini' Maida shi").Result()
? cCandidate
#--> JIBINI
aV = oKH.ReplyIn("c", cCandidate)
? aV[:narration]
#--> admitted: 'pizza' contains 'jibini'

ran: printed what this block promises

Third, the question in the learner's language. The tutor is a consumer of the conversation: it uses the gap the conversation names, and it chooses the words to say it in four languages. The sentences are templates. The code's own comment says that the French, Arabic and Hausa wording is a draft awaiting a native reviewer, so read the three below as drafts, and not as reviewed text:

Haro
oEx = StzProgramQ("../../education/program").CourseQ("elementary-introduction").ExerciseQ("ex-01-01")
? oEx.GapText("finds", "en")
#--> Where are the repeated items? Which line of your program asks for their positions? (why: the mental model finds before it applies)
? oEx.GapText("finds", "fr")
#--> Où sont les éléments répétés ? Quelle ligne de votre programme demande leurs positions ? (pourquoi : le modèle mental trouve avant d'agir)
? oEx.GapText("finds", "ar")
#--> أين العناصر المكررة؟ أيّ سطر في برنامجك يسأل عن مواضعها؟ (لماذا: النموذج الذهني يبحث قبل أن يطبّق)
? oEx.GapText("finds", "ha")
#--> Ina abubuwan da aka maimaita? Wane layi a shirinka yake tambayar wurarensu? (dalili: tsarin tunani yana nemo kafin ya aiwatar)

So the library cannot ask in Arabic or in Hausa through AskIn. What it can do is hold the data in any script, take a candidate computed in any pack, and let the tutor say the gap in four languages. A reply that has a space in it raises at the moment, and so the connectors "et" in French, "da" in Hausa and "و" in Arabic are not connectors. May the chapter print it as it stands, with that caveat, or will you give the Arabic and the Hausa you want shown?]

A model is a fluency, never the mind

Without a model, a conversation stays on its deterministic floor and says so. The word "neural" can be set, and it is claimed only when a model is really there:

Haro
oKF2 = new stzKnowledgeGraph("fluency-space")
oKF2.AddConversation("f")
? oKF2.ConversationQ("f").Fluency()
#--> plain
oKF2.ConversationQ("f").SetFluency(:neural)
? oKF2.ConversationQ("f").Fluency()
#--> neural
? oKF2.ConversationQ("f").IsFluencyNeural()
#--> 0

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused to guess. The record's phrase is: guessing is replaced by asking, and vibes are replaced by governance. A gap is a question. A reply is a candidate.

I refused a different gate for each way of answering. A formula is not trusted because it is code, and a structure is not trusted because it is typed. The form does not buy trust. All five registers land in one funnel.

I refused a stub. A reserved agent raises when it is asked for. The design document says it plainly: the raise is the law working, and it should not be read as a defect. I refused to pretend the fifth register works.

I refused an agent that fills a gap to finish the job. The wise coder stops, and leaves the gap for a person.

I refused to let a conversation own a world. It happens inside a knowledge space and never owns one, and a copy of the knowledge held in a session goes stale. That is the reason every call above is chained from the space.

I refused a deleted checkpoint. Expiry takes a refusal off the live list. The record keeps it.

I refused to let the example look like the answer. The record's closing law about the fifth register is that an admitted candidate writes its example back as a promise. That law is designed, and not built. [AUTHOR: The code wires three of five registers; the memo that names the formula and the examples calls them filed and not routed. Does the chapter say they are the next work you have filed, or only that they are absent?]

5. The court

wisecoding_narrated proves that the gap is computed from the space; that the question is led by the system, names its subject and says why it asks; that "X and Y" and a data structure admit; that a unique law refuses through the conversation and the refusal reaches a checkpoint; and that concluding with a gap open is refused. wisecoding_rich_narrated proves the goal monitored to fulfilled or revoked, the frame, the numbered options and the refusal of a number nobody offered, the lifetime of a checkpoint, and the fluency that is claimed only with a model. ownagentstack_narrated proves the roster of five, the wired wise coder, the reserved agent that raises, and the gap left for a person. tutor_gaps_narrated proves the exercise's gap question in each language, and that a step with no question in a language is red, never another language. It writes folders, so the book counts it and does not run it; the last block above only reads the course.

The guards end by calling a function that prints the total and then stops the run with a raise. That is the guard's way to end.

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in understanding. A dialogue framework reads free text with trained models, speaks on many channels and ships connectors. The record says what Softanza lacks, in its own count: the word "WhatsApp" appears in no code file and no design document of the library. The conversation asks one slot at a time, over a graph the user must first have declared, and it does not understand an open reply.

The field leads on examples. Programming by example is shipped in spreadsheets today. Softanza has no induction at all, and the record says so: nothing induces yet. A search for "induce", "from examples" and "infer" over the regular-expression folder finds nothing.

The field is honest about costs, and so is the record. Several candidates is the normal case when you ask for a rule from examples. A pattern induced from three examples overfits them. The remedy the record names is the question that tells two candidates apart. And the index that would carry the examples is as clean as the tags of the methods, with about eighty-five misspellings.

Where I think the record stands apart: every reply, in whatever form, is judged by the world's laws before it counts, with the reason, and the session keeps a transcript and a checkpoint that a person can read. The field's reply is a prompt, and the human keeps what comes out.

7. The limit

  • builtthe goal, the gap and the question with its reason; a reply as an option, a data structure or a sentence split on commas and the word 'and'; the governed door with its refusals; the checkpoint with its lifetime; the goal fulfilled or revoked; one wired agent that stops where it would have to invent
  • designedseveral readings of one reply, enumerated for the person to choose; the nearest alternatives named after a refusal; the example written back as a promise
  • absentthe formula register; the example register; a conversation whose question is worded in Arabic, Hausa or French; a reply with a space in it

What is built: the goal, the gap, the question with its reason, the frame; the first register, the second, and the fourth in the form of a splitter; the governed door with its refusals; the checkpoint and its lifetime; the goal fulfilled or revoked; the transcript; one wired agent; the tutor's four-language gap sentence.

What is designed: the several acceptable branch as the design writes it. The protocol says that when several readings of a reply are acceptable, the system enumerates them and the person chooses. What is built is two different things: the values already known become numbered options in the question, before the reply; and a reply that carries several values has each one judged on its own, with the first kept under a unique law. No step presents competing readings of one reply. And the none acceptable branch as written: the reason is built, and the nearest acceptable alternatives are not. The refusal states a reason, and for a number, how many options were on the table. The site's two pages on this, wise and by example, say "with the nearest alternatives" and "the person chooses", and the pages say more than the code does. [AUTHOR: May the chapter say outright that the two pages promise more than the code, so that the page or the code is corrected?]

What is absent: the formula register; the example register, and the induction agent behind it; a conversation worded in Arabic, Hausa or French; and a reply with a space in it. In the version of the library this book runs, ReplyIn raises, with an uninitialised variable, on any value containing a space: "tomato sauce", "fromage et tomate", "jibini da tumatir". The direct call to the door returns the refusal properly. The conversation should have refused with the reason and written a checkpoint, and it doesn't. It is in the memo as a request, and the exercise below does not use a reply with a space.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerA reply is a verdict you can test with ordinary promises: what was admitted, what was refused, and the state of the goal.
The analystThe goal is the schema of a complete model. The gaps are the list of what is missing. The transcript and the checkpoints are the evidence of how each fact got in.
The designerThe question comes back as data: force, subject, relation, options, reason. Any medium can render it. The library renders English, and the tutor shows the pattern for four languages.
The decision-makerA reply is judged before it counts. A refusal reaches a person with its context and a lifetime. The roster is honest: one agent of five is wired, and two of the five registers are not available.
The educatorThe tutor is wise coding. It names the missing step as a question and never as the answer, in the learner's language, and its wording in three of those languages awaits a native reviewer.
The agentYou can drive the loop yourself with an answer source, and you must stop where you would have to invent. You cannot offer examples and be understood, and you are told by name when you ask for a reserved agent.

9. Exercise

Choose a small world of your own, a shop, a class, a clinic, with four entities of one type and a goal that each needs one relation. Before you run anything, write under each of the replies below the verdict you expect, admitted, refused with a reason, or neither:

  1. a plain word;
  2. a second word, offered as a number after the first is known;
  3. a number nobody offered;
  4. two values at once, for a relation you have declared unique;
  5. a list of two pairs of examples.

Then run it. If a promise breaks, do not change the promise: explain the output first.

Part IV · Chapter 19

The domain language model

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-09 02:32 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 7 of 7 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

A language model predicts the next token. A token is a fragment of text with no type, no role and no constraint: it can be the end of a word, a space, a bracket. Everything a model says is built by choosing tokens one after another, and everything that makes the result useful, that it is a valid sentence, that it is true, that it fits a schema, is checked afterwards or enforced from outside.

The field has made this work with three tools. You adapt a general model to a domain by training it further on the domain's documents. You give it the relevant documents at the moment of the question, retrieved by similarity. And you constrain its decoding with a grammar, so that it cannot produce a malformed sentence, as chapter 11 showed. All three keep the unit the same: the token.

2. The first principle

The next thing the model says is a checkable unit of your world, a fact your rules admit or refuse, never a token. And the gate is the same for every model of this kind: generations are proposals, and the graph and its rules decide admission.

3. The Softanza form

I call it a domain language model, and it has two rungs. The first has no neurons at all and was shown in chapter 17: it answers from recorded facts, says why, and refuses outside its domain. The second is a small neural model, optional, which gives it fluency. Both end at the same gate.

Begin with where the training text comes from. No one writes it. Each sentence is a fact of the knowledge base, rendered, and the vocabulary is closed: every word the domain holds, with a first entry for the unknown.

Haro
oKB = new stzKnowledgeGraph("restaurant")
oKB.Know("margherita", "dish").
    Know("tiramisu", "dish").
    Know("chianti", "wine").
    KnowRelation("margherita", "contains", "tomato-sauce").
    KnowRelation("margherita", "contains", "mozzarella").
    KnowRelation("margherita", "pairs-with", "chianti")
oDLM = StzDlmQ(oKB)
? @@( oDLM.GenerateCorpus() )
#--> [ "margherita is a dish.", "tiramisu is a dish.", "chianti is a wine.", "margherita contains tomato-sauce.", "margherita contains mozzarella.", "margherita pairs-with chianti." ]
? @@( oDLM.Tokenizer() )
#--> [ "<unk>", "margherita", "tiramisu", "chianti", "dish", "wine", "contains", "pairs-with", "is", "a", "tomato-sauce", "mozzarella" ]
? @@( oDLM.Tokenize("margherita contains something-new") )
#--> [ 2, 7, 1 ]

ran: printed what this block promises

Twelve words, and a word outside the domain maps to the first one. "Correct by construction" holds here in the one sense the code gives it: each sentence is a recorded fact. It does not yet hold in the sense the design intended; section 7 says where.

Completion is constrained to the domain: after an entity, only its relations; after a relation, only its objects; a fragment completes to entities; a word that the domain does not hold completes to nothing.

Haro
? @@( oDLM.Complete("margherita") )
#--> [ "contains", "pairs-with" ]
? @@( oDLM.Complete("contains") )
#--> [ "tomato-sauce", "mozzarella" ]
? @@( oDLM.Complete("tira") )
#--> [ "tiramisu" ]
? @@( oDLM.Complete("pizza") )
#--> [ ]

ran: printed what this block promises

I have to say what this is, because the guard that proves it calls it "the grammar spirit". It is a lookup in the facts, not decoding under a compiled grammar. And it sees one word, not the sentence so far: Complete("contains") returns the objects of every contains fact, whatever its subject.

The grammar itself can be derived from the knowledge base, and here the reader of this book has to write the derivation. There is no call in the library that turns a knowledge base into a grammar, and the design lists it as the first rung's task. But the pieces compose. The domain's vocabulary becomes the choices of a schema from chapter 11, the schema compiles to a grammar, and the grammar has no path for a word outside the domain:

Haro
aLex = oDLM.Lexicon()
acObjects = []
for aFact in oKB.Facts()
	if aFact[2] != "is-a" and find(acObjects, aFact[3]) = 0
		acObjects + aFact[3]
	ok
next
oS = StzOutputSchemaQ([
	[ :field = "subject",  :type = :oneof, :choices = aLex[:entities] ],
	[ :field = "relation", :type = :oneof, :choices = aLex[:relations] ],
	[ :field = "object",   :type = :oneof, :choices = acObjects ]
])
? oS.ToGBNF()
#--> root ::= subject-line relation-line object-line
#    subject-line ::= "subject: " ("margherita" | "tiramisu" | "chianti") "\n"
#    relation-line ::= "relation: " ("contains" | "pairs-with") "\n"
#    object-line ::= "object: " ("tomato-sauce" | "mozzarella" | "chianti") "\n"
#    text ::= [^\n]+
#    number ::= "-"? [0-9]+ ("." [0-9]+)?
#    boolean ::= ("yes" | "no" | "true" | "false")
cGood = "subject: margherita" + nl + "relation: contains" + nl + "object: mozzarella" + nl
cOut  = "subject: pizza" + nl + "relation: contains" + nl + "object: mozzarella" + nl
cLie  = "subject: tiramisu" + nl + "relation: contains" + nl + "object: mozzarella" + nl
? oS.Accepts(cGood)
#--> 1
? oS.Accepts(cOut)
#--> 0
? oS.Accepts(cLie)
#--> 1
? oDLM.Ask("tiramisu contains what?")
#--> I hold no 'contains' knowledge about 'tiramisu'.

ran: printed what this block promises

Look at the last four lines together. The grammar accepts the sentence that says a tiramisu contains mozzarella, because it has the right shape and every word is in the domain. The model refuses it, because the graph holds no such fact. A grammar is a gate for shape; the truth belongs to the graph.

A domain language model is a file that travels. It is saved as plain text, readable and diff-able, with no binary and no weights, and a second model that has never seen the knowledge base can answer from it and run its own tests:

Haro
oDLM.AddGolden("what is margherita", "Margherita is a dish.")
oDLM.AddGolden("what is the weather today?",
	"That is outside the 'restaurant' domain (I know 3 entities and 2 relations).")
cFile = oDLM.Save("probe_dlm")
? cFile
#--> probe_dlm.zdlm
? read(cFile)
#--> dlm "restaurant"
#    entities
#        margherita | dish
#        tiramisu | dish
#        chianti | wine
#    relations
#        contains
#        pairs-with
#    facts
#        margherita | contains | tomato-sauce
#        margherita | contains | mozzarella
#        margherita | pairs-with | chianti
#    laws
#    goldens
#        what is margherita | Margherita is a dish.
#        what is the weather today? | That is outside the 'restaurant' domain (I know 3 entities and 2 relations).
oShipped = StzDlmQ("")
oShipped.LoadFrom(cFile)
? oShipped.Ask("what is tiramisu")
#--> Tiramisu is a dish.
? @@( oShipped.RunGoldens() )
#--> [ [ "total", 2 ], [ "passed", 2 ], [ "failed", [ ] ] ]
remove(cFile)
? fexists(cFile)
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

this block touches files; the output shown was recorded on 2026-10-09 02:30 UTC+01:00

The refusal travels with the bundle as a golden test, and the second model, which has never seen the graph, passes it. The laws section is empty because no law was declared before the model was forged; declare that a relation is unique, forge again, and the line appears.

Now the second rung. It is a small neural model trained on the corpus you saw, with no teacher, and it can be exported as a model file. I will tell its size in the same breath as its result, because it is small: a single layer that learns to predict the next word from the previous one, over twelve words, trained on fifteen pairs.

Haro
oDLM.TrainNeuralRung(500)
? oDLM.NeuralWhy()
#--> neural bigram rung: 15 pairs over a 12-word vocab; trained 500 epoch(s), lr 0.50: loss 2.57 -> 0.70
? oDLM.NextToken("is")
#--> a
? oDLM.NextTokenConfidence("is")
#--> 1.00
cGguf = oDLM.ExportNeuralGguf("probe_bigram")
? cGguf
#--> probe_bigram.gguf
? StzEngineNeuralGgufInspect(cGguf)
#--> 2
remove(cGguf)

ran: printed what this block promises

this block touches files; the output shown was recorded on 2026-10-09 02:30 UTC+01:00

The file holds two tensors, a weight and a bias, and the library can read it back. I do not claim another runtime loads it as a text generator. It trains in a fraction of a second, offline, and gives the same numbers on every run.

What does a model like this say? It is fluent in the grammar of the domain, and it is wrong about facts. That is the reason for the gate:

Haro
aCorpus = oDLM.GenerateCorpus()
for cSeed in [ "tiramisu", "chianti", "margherita" ]
	cSaid = oDLM.NeuralGenerate(cSeed, 3)
	? cSaid + "  ->  " + ( find(aCorpus, cSaid + ".") > 0 )
next
#--> tiramisu is a wine  ->  0
#    chianti is a wine  ->  1
#    margherita contains mozzarella is  ->  0

ran: printed what this block promises

"Tiramisu is a wine" is false, because tiramisu is a dish. "Chianti is a wine" is true. And "margherita contains mozzarella is" is a run-on, because the bigram has no word that ends a sentence. The test against the corpus is a crude gate, and it would refuse a true fact nobody recorded. The real gate is the graph and its laws:

Haro
oKB.ConstrainRelation("is-a", :Unique)
aVerdict = oKB.Admit("tiramisu", "is-a", "wine", [ :source = "rung 2" ])
? aVerdict[:admitted]
#--> 0
? aVerdict[:why]
#--> 'tiramisu' already bears 'is-a' (to 'dish'); the relation is :Unique
? @@( oKB.Contradictions() )
#--> [ [ [ "subject", "tiramisu" ], [ "relation", "is-a" ], [ "existing", "dish" ], [ "attempted", "wine" ], [ "source", "rung 2" ] ] ]
? oKB.Admit("pizza", "is-a", "dish", [ :source = "rung 2" ])[:why]
#--> admitted: 'pizza' is-a 'dish'

ran: printed what this block promises

The false proposal is refused with its reason, and the refusal is kept, with its source: the model's second rung. A new fact is admitted. That is the whole of the principle in seven lines: a proposal, a law, a refusal with its why, and the refusal on the record.

The design describes the unit of prediction in three levels. A token is a fragment with no type. An embedding is a vector without a role. And a chunk is a typed node of a graph, with a tag, a payload and edges: a declaration, a relationship, a constraint. A chunk is validated in five stages before it enters the graph: type, pattern, graph integrity, compliance, and constructive contribution. I tell it as design, because there is no chunk in the library. What exists are pieces: the court of chapter 11 checks a text's type and shape; the admission above enforces a law, which is compliance; and adding a fact twice is a harmless no-op, which is a small form of the last stage. Nothing chains them.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

On 13 July 2026, I ruled on this. The concept of a domain language model had been designed for one of the estate's products; I donated it to the open foundation, so that any Softanza project that supplies a knowledge base can ship its own model free to the users of its domain. The format is .zdlm. The floor is the first rung, in every model; the second is optional fluency. [AUTHOR: The record has your ruling that a model is free to ship, and no licence text to say so. May the book tell "free" as: a plain file, in the open foundation, with no licence fee or meter?]

I refused the token as the unit. The unit is a chunk of the world, which a graph can admit or refuse.

I refused a teacher I cannot see. The earlier design of the idea used a large commercial model to write its training corpus. I put a law against it, and this model's corpus is rendered from the domain's own facts: the library's second law says a capability never requires anything paid or remote.

I refused neural first. The finding the section starts from is that the canonical model is not neural. A review of the earlier product archived a transformer of one to three billion parameters, in favour of rule-based prediction, on the ground that hallucination is impossible when the model cannot generate almost-valid text. So the first rung has zero training and zero cost, and the neural rung comes second.

I refused to let the shape stand for the truth. The grammar says structure kills malformedness, not falsehood. The truth belongs to the graph, to its laws, and to a person.

5. The court

dlm_narrated proves the model forged from a graph, its answers with their why, its refusal outside the domain, the completion, the plain-text bundle with its goldens, the closed tokenizer and the second rung with its model file. One of its assertions on the second rung checks only that the generated sentence begins with a fixed prefix, so it would also pass the false sentence above. structuredoutput_narrated, schema_grammar_narrated and constrained_decoding_narrated prove the court of chapter 11, the grammar compiler and the sampler; the last of them has two scenes that need a generative model file, which this machine does not hold, so only part of it ran for this page. knowledge_integration_narrated proves derivation and the refusal by a law. And I should say that the admission I show in the last block is not called by its name in any guard: it is reached through the conversation, and by the strict form of adding a fact, which the guard does assert.

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in scale. Training and serving models of every size is a mature practice; this second rung is a single layer over twelve words, and the steps that would make it more, a validated corpus, deduplication, a trained tokenizer, a larger network, quantisation, are not done. I do not compete with large models.

The field leads in fluency, which is the point of a model. A first rung that answers from facts will say "I hold no knowledge about that" where a general model would write something plausible, and for a customer the plausible thing is often more useful. The record's own answer is the second rung, and its present state is the table above.

Where I think this stands apart is in what the output is. A general model's answer is text, and every check on it is after the fact. Here every answer of the first rung carries its why and a certainty of one, and every proposal of the second meets a gate that can refuse it with a reason. A model that can only say what the domain holds, and a gate that remembers what it refused: that is what a bank, a ministry or a school can sign.

7. The limit

  • builtthe domain model's first rung with no neurons; its facts rendered as a corpus; a closed vocabulary; completion by lookup; a plain-text bundle that travels with its tests; a small second rung, a bigram, exported to a model file; the admission of a fact by a law
  • designeda grammar derived from a knowledge base by one call; the typed unit of prediction validated in five stages; a second rung whose corpus is checked before it trains; the foundry that would make it larger
  • absenta pipeline that chains the five stages on any unit; an end-of-sentence word for the second rung; a completion that sees the sentence so far

What is built: the first rung and its answers; the facts rendered as a corpus, with a closed vocabulary; completion by lookup; the bundle that travels with its tests; a second rung that trains in a fraction of a second and exports a small model file; and the admission of a fact by a law.

What is designed, and the page must say each:

  • The grammar derived from a knowledge base by one call. Chapter 19's composition is the reader's, not the library's.
  • The second rung's corpus validated by the first rung's grammar before it is admitted. The design says so; the code renders the facts directly, with no such check. So "correct by construction" holds for the training text, and not for what the model says.
  • The five-stage validation of a chunk. None exists as a pipeline.
  • The foundry's steps beyond the bigram.

What is absent: an end-of-sentence word for the second rung, which is why one of its sentences runs on; and a completion that sees the sentence so far, which is why a completion after a relation lists the objects of every fact of that relation. The first rung also answers a rephrased question with the type, as chapter 17 showed, where the law of this part says it should refuse.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerA model is a file you can read, diff and test: its facts, its laws and its goldens.
The analystA fact you add makes the model know more, and a law you add makes it refuse more, with no training.
The designerThe model's refusal is part of its contract: the golden test says what it must decline to answer.
The decision-makerThe model can only say what the domain holds, and the gate keeps the record of what it refused and why.
The educatorRung one is a model a learner can read in full. Rung two is small enough to train in front of a class.
The agentWhat you propose is a fact the graph can admit or refuse, with a reason you can read.

9. Exercise

Forge a domain of your own with three entities and two relations. Before you run anything, write what you expect from three calls: the completion of an entity, the completion of a relation, and the answer to a question about a thing the domain does not hold. Then declare that one relation is unique and propose, in the form of a fact, something that contradicts it.

Run it. Then write a sentence of the right shape and the wrong truth, and say which of the grammar and the graph refuses it, and which does not.

Agents that cannot hurt you

1. The concept, as the field holds it

In the field, safety is a property of the agent. The doctrine document of the library lists what the field offers: alignment, guardrails, confirmation prompts, a checkbox that says a human is in the loop. Tool-using agents, and the families that descend from the first of them, let the model's tool calls touch reality immediately, with a prompt for confirmation. Computer-use agents run in a sandboxed virtual machine, which contains a process, and does not tell a file moved from random bytes churning.

The best advice of the field, repeated in every serious guide of 2026, is to separate planning from execution and put a human approval between them. It is good advice, and it is advice: a pattern you implement, and can forget. The threat lists of the field, the OWASP list of risks for agentic applications among them, are lenses, and the record uses them so.

So the field's posture, in a line, is that the agent is a model in a loop, and safety is vigilance around it. (General knowledge, not a study of the record, except where I name the document.) Chapter 17 said this of the whole mind. This chapter takes the action half: what happens when the proposal meets the world.

2. The first principle

Do not build safe agents. Build a safe world, and let ordinary agents loose inside it.

The sentence is in the library's doctrine document: "We will not build safe agents. We will build a safe world, and let ordinary agents loose inside it." The document gives its structural half in one more: the only artifact that ever leaves its world is an update plan, and plans are executed by someone else. [AUTHOR: The doctrine document carries no date and no author line in its header, and git first records it in a commit of 9 July 2026. Is the sentence yours, may the chapter open on it in the first person, and when was it written?]

3. The Softanza form

Four steps, in the form the study of the record gives them: the agent proposes, the workbench rehearses, the court judges, and only a governed actor commits. I will show each in code, and then the cases where a step does not hold.

May this agent exist? Before an agent runs a single tick, the governance asks the question, and it asks it when the answer is free. An agent that declares no coverage, one sentence saying what it covers, is refused. An agent that declares no reversibility class is refused too: reversible, compensable or irreversible. Both refusals are in the engine's own sentences, and the Ring door repeats them.

Haro
oGov = new stzGovernance("shop")
oGov.DeclareReversibility("restocker", :Compensable)
? oGov.ReversibilityOf("restocker")
#--> compensable
? oGov.MayRegister("mystery", "", "reversible")
#--> 0
? oGov.Why()
#--> AGENTLOOP-R4: agent 'mystery' declares no coverage statement. Registration refuses it. Say what this agent covers, in one sentence, before the loop will run it. Law 18: nothing schedules what nobody has stated the reach of.
? oGov.MayRegister("mystery", "reorders stock", "")
#--> 0
? oGov.Why()
#--> AGENTLOOP-R5: agent 'mystery' declares no reversibility class. Registration refuses it. Declare one of: reversible | compensable | irreversible. Law 18: an agent whose reversal nobody stated cannot be scheduled by something that cannot undo it.
? oGov.MayRegister("mystery", "reorders stock", :Compensable)
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

Reversibility is the sixth contract of the governance, beside risk, authority, commitment, decommission and lineage. It is orthogonal to risk: an act of small risk that cannot be undone deserves more ceremony than a large one that can.

The harder an act is to undo, the more trusted the code that does it must be. Here is the whole table, the posture of the code against the class of the act, printed by a loop of the book's own:

Haro
aPostures = [ "trusted", "external", "sandboxed" ]
aClasses = [ "reversible", "compensable", "irreversible" ]
for cP in aPostures
	cRow = cP + ":"
	for cC in aClasses
		if StzPostureReversibilityRefusal(cP, cC) = ""
			cRow += " yes"
		else
			cRow += " no"
		ok
	next
	? cRow
next
#--> trusted: yes yes yes
#--> external: yes yes no
#--> sandboxed: yes no no
? StzPostureReversibilityRefusal("sandboxed", "irreversible")
#--> a 'sandboxed' posture does not cover 'irreversible' work -- the harder an act is to undo, the more trusted the code performing it must be (reversibility x posture, ruling 3.2)

Two lines of the file decide who may act. posture: trusted is there because a ring: clause must carry a posture, and StzAllowAgentFunction is the platform's code, and not the agent's file, deciding which functions a file may call.

The only export is a plan, and it narrates itself. The tick exports toward reality a plan and nothing else. The plan says what it would do before anything is attempted. A language model set as its executor is refused before any attempt, because it lacks the capability to produce an effect. A named actor under a scope that does not cover the path commits nothing: the disk still did not move. The same actor under a scope that covers the path commits once, and the audit trail names the actor. Reality changes here and only here:

? StzReplace(oPlan.Narration(), cFx, "<fixture>")
#--> Update plan (1 of 1 operations to commit):

oPlan.SetExecutor(LLMActor("eager-llm"))
? oPlan.MayCommit()[2]

oScope = new stzCommitScope()
oScope.AllowUnder("/somewhere/else")
oPlan2 = oAg.GenerateUpdatePlan()
oPlan2.SetExecutor(PIActor("shop-committer"))
oPlan2.SetScope(oScope)

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused safe agents. The doctrine's reason is that the field's safety tries to make a fundamentally unpredictable actor trustworthy. Asking whether the agent might escape is like asking whether a chess engine might move a piece on a physical board: the agent's tool surface contains no operation that touches the disk, a database or the network.

I refused a permission check as the boundary. It is not a check that the agent might route around. The powers are separated: creativity without authority, authority without creativity.

I refused a second workbench for machines. The sandbox is the same workbench that the human programmer already uses. The framework was conceived for human programmers, and everything designed to liberate one is exactly what is needed to contain an artificial one.

I refused to leave the gate optional. The ruling of 22 August 2026 says the registration gate is doctrine, and that opting in is a migration state, not the design. The record is honest about the finding behind the ruling: where the doctrine of agents that cannot hurt you bound that day was nowhere. The safe world existed, and the agentic folder did not mention any of it. The ruling closed it the same day.

I refused a stub. Asking for a reserved agent raises. The architecture says that this is the law working, and not a defect.

I refused to drop quietly. In the engine, a send to a full inbox is refused with a code and counted. When the run queue is full, further visits are dropped and counted. The loop also states what it cannot see: the inside of a callback, the clock, and whether a coverage statement is true.

I refused to let a machine be the last resort. The interface constitution of the estate has a right, the sixth of six: the Right to a Human. Wherever a machine serves, a person is reachable, clearly, and without penalty. It is enforced by judgment, a person's, and not by a guard that runs; the library does not mention it. [AUTHOR: Do you want the chapter to say so in those words and to state the right as the human end of the loop, or to leave a one-line pointer to the interface constitution?]

5. The court

safeworld_narrated has seven scenes: reversibility as the sixth contract; the registration gate in the engine's sentences; the table of posture against reversibility; the file's court at load; what the file declares landing in the agent's governance; the workbench, from the disk that did not move to the audit trail; and the roster's agent rehearsed and then committed. agentfile_narrated proves that an agent is a file judged at load, with one refusal per gate, and that a folder is a deployment. agentloop_engine_narrated proves that the engine loop states its coverage at run time, that registration is a gate, that one rule gives the same words in two layers, and that an over-full queue drops visits and counts them. containment_drill_narrated proves a drill against a real target on loopback: a model investigator proposes the containment and commits nothing; a human commits, and containment holds when verified from outside. In the run I made on 8 October 2026 the drill read 443 ms to detect and 61 ms to contain, on this machine. The site prints other numbers from its own run, and the threat model others from its own, and the three differ because the drill measures a clock. The limit of the drill is one attack shape, on loopback, on one machine, run on demand. virtual_system_twin_narrated proves the twin: a rehearsal touches nothing real; the plan narrates and flags its risks; a scope refuses; a reviewer rejects a step; snapshots roll back.

The guard roster_narrated is not in the front matter, because it cannot run from a snapshot of the library: it loads the estate's roster files from a sibling repository. The rehearsal of the roster's agent is proved by safeworld_narrated, whose seventh scene is the last block above.

6. The field, and where it leads

The record's own table is honest, and I carry its rows in prose.

The field leads in connectors: chat, drives and trackers a few clicks away, hosted vector stores, streaming interfaces. They are reachable from Softanza and not paved.

The field leads in retrieval over open corpora. Softanza wins on a curated domain and loses on the open web.

The field leads in frontier reasoning. That stack orchestrates the largest models on every call.

The field leads in ecosystem and hiring. There is a labour market for that stack, and none for this one.

When to reach for which, in the narration's words: the mainstream stack, when the task is open-ended language work over material you cannot curate, such as summarising arbitrary documents, conversational products, research over the open web. The Softanza layer, when actions have consequences and someone will eventually ask why it did that: regulated work, anything unattended, anything offline at zero marginal cost. The two are not exclusive, and a model can sit inside a Softanza system as a proposer.

The twin is a model of reality, not reality. The framework asks for fidelity and honesty, and the plan re-validates against reality before it is committed: after the real file is deleted behind the twin's back, the validation says the target is absent in reality. I saw it warn, and did not test whether it blocks the commit.

And the largest honest loss. The threat model puts code already running in the process out of scope: it can do anything the process can, wipe the ledger or read a secret. The workbench contains what is written through the bench. A function that does not ask for the bench is not confined. Reads are free. The architecture says that the escape is not a defect to be closed by removing it, and it narrows it with a declared posture, and with code, not the file, deciding which functions an agent may call. I did not run a trusted function that bypasses the bench: I read this limit in the architecture and the threat model.

7. The limit

  • builtreversibility as a declared contract and a registration gate; posture set against reversibility, at the door and at load; the workbench, the plan, the reviewer's rejection, the committing actor under a scope; the containment drill; the engine's bounded slots, inbox and queue
  • designedthe agent's side of the negotiation over a plan; the examination hall; branches as parallel minds; twins for databases, interfaces and networks
  • absenta plan with no executor that is refused; a ranking of a plan's risks; code already running in the process, which is out of scope; the Right to a Human as a machine check

What is built: reversibility as a declared contract, and the registration gate, in the Ring door and in the engine; posture set against reversibility at the door and at load; the workbench, with a plan that narrates, flags, validates, takes a rejection and keeps an audit trail; the roster's agent rehearsed and then committed; the drill; the engine's bounded structures, which are 64 agent slots, an inbox of 8 messages and a run queue of 256.

What is designed: the agent's side of the negotiation, in which the plan reaches the agent but the conversation about the plan does not yet. The architecture says so, and the threat model repeats it. I searched the library's code and found no revising of a plan. The examination hall, which would certify an agent for a commit scope the way you certify a driver for a licence class: it occurs in documents and in no code. Branches as parallel minds: snapshots and rollback are built, and I found no branch call. Twins for databases, interfaces and networks: the framework names them. The twin of files is built, and so is the twin of the process environment, with its variables, its working directory and its queued spawn (chapter 24). The other three are not.

What is a gap, found while running and reading:

  • An unset executor is unguarded. A plan with no executor answers that no executor is set, and that a human at the keyboard is unguarded, and Execute() is allowed. The refusal of the block above applies to a model set as the executor. So "only a governed actor commits" is exact when an executor is set, and a person at a keyboard may commit a plan that names none.
  • A plan flags; it does not rank. The narration says that a plan ranks its own risks. The code returns one flag per destructive step, in the order of the operations, with a label such as DESTRUCTIVE. There is no score and no order of severity. The chapter says "flags".
  • The gate is opt-in at the host. The default flips when the last host in the tree declares. A fresh host runs the older pump.
  • The loop checks that a coverage statement exists, not that it is true.
  • The drill's limits: one shape of attack, on loopback, on one machine.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerYour agent is a file and a few functions. It runs and believes it acted, and the disk does not move. You read the plan, choose the committing actor and the scope, and the court tells you in one sentence which rule refused you.
The analystEvery proposal is a narrated plan of operations with the destructive steps flagged, and an audit line for each commit. You can read what the agent meant to do, step by step, without running it. The flags are by kind, not scored.
The designerThe plan is the one artefact that crosses from the agent to the person, and a person can reject one step. The Right to a Human says a person is reachable wherever a machine serves, and the right is held by judgment.
The decision-makerYou declare what each agent covers and how reversible it is before it may exist, and you decide the scope and the actor that commits. A model is structurally unable to commit, even when fooled; the threat model assumes it will be. The hardest part is the one the design leaves to you: which functions code allows an agent to call.
The educatorA learner's agent that tidies a course folder by deleting everything is a lesson in what a plan is. She sees what it would have done, and the files are still there.
The agentYou may rehearse without limit, inside the twin. Your only export is a plan, and you can be argued with over it. You may not commit. Today the argument is one-way: you do not yet receive the reviewer's objection and revise.

9. Exercise

Choose a folder of ten files you could lose. Write an agent file for a tidy-up job on it: what it covers, how reversible it is, one skill. Before you run anything, write under each line the promise you expect: how many files exist on disk after one cycle; how many operations the plan holds; how many of them the plan flags as risks; and what happens when you set a language model as the executor.

Haro
cDirMine = StzReplace(WorkingDirectory(), "\", "/") + "/_mine"
StzDirCreatePath(cDirMine)
for i = 1 to 10
	StzFileWrite(cDirMine + "/file" + i + ".txt", "file " + i)
next
oMine = new stzVirtualFileSystem()
oMine.SetActor("my-tidy-bot")
# your tidy-up proposal here, with the promise you expect under each line
StzDirDeleteAll(cDirMine)

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Run it. Then give the plan to a committing actor under a scope that does not cover the folder, and write the promise again. If a promise breaks, do not change the promise: explain the output first. A good learner is surprised once. The plan flags its destructive steps and does not rank them, and a plan with no executor at all is allowed.

The court: promises, perception, security and performance

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-09 02:33 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 7 of 7 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

Four practices of the field are four courts, and they are rarely seen as one.

The first is the example that runs. Python's doctest runs the interactive session found in a docstring and compares the printed text. Rust runs the examples in its documentation, and Go has testable examples with an expected output in a comment. The example is the specification. Its weakness is that the comparison is text against text, and the harness decides what a failure is.

The second is the snapshot test. A screenshot or a rendered tree is stored and compared on the next run. It proves that today's picture equals yesterday's.

The third is the audit against a list. The field's lists are OWASP's, NIST's and the compliance frameworks'. For detection and evidence, the toolchain is the log aggregator, the rule format, the orchestration of responses.

The fourth is the instrument. Micrometer, OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and the profilers of every runtime measure a program from the outside. (General knowledge, not a study of the record, except where I name the file.)

2. The first principle

A claim is only as good as the court that can refuse it. And where no court can see, the record says so.

The record has it in two sentences that meet. The threat model: every guarantee names the guard that proves it, and a guarantee without a guard is listed as an open risk. And the perception law: a comparison proves sameness and never rightness, and if a person is the last consumer, a person is the last gate. Under both lies the doctrine that the library repeats in every plane: expression is free, and admission is governed.

3. The Softanza form

Chapter 5 told the court that judges whoever wrote the code. This chapter has four courts, one per kind of claim. I show each by something it refuses.

The court of promises

A promise in this book is the line #--> under an expression, and it is a claim about a stop of the program. The tool that reads it, called the traveller, says a promise is kept, diverged, unreached or unjudged. A promise that argues with itself, prose after a value, is never accused. The runner's exit code is the runner's, and not the language's:

Haro
write("tour.haro", '? 1 + 1' + nl + '#--> 2' + nl +
	'? 1 + 1' + nl + '#--> 3' + nl +
	'? "C"  #--> "C" but should be "sm_AS"' + nl)
oTour = TravellerQ().Silent().Walk("tour.haro")
aClaims = oTour.Records()[1][:run][:stops][1][:claims]
? aClaims[1][:state]
#--> kept
? aClaims[2][:state]
#--> diverged
? aClaims[3][:state]
#--> unjudged
? oTour.ExitCode()
#--> 1
remove("tour.haro")

A promise can be that the line raises. That is read as a raise that was promised. When it happens, the promise is kept and the tour has finished as it said it would, even though the language process ended with an error:

Haro
write("raise.haro", '? "before"  #--> before' + nl +
	'? Boom()  #--> ERROR: boom happened' + nl +
	'func Boom()' + nl + char(9) + 'raise("boom happened")' + nl)
oRaise = TravellerQ().Silent().Walk("raise.haro")
aRun = oRaise.Records()[1][:run]
? aRun[:stops][1][:claims][2][:state]
#--> kept
? aRun[:end]
#--> finished
? oRaise.ExitCode()
#--> 0
remove("raise.haro")

Every rule of this judge was learned by watching the harness accuse the library falsely. The guard's header says it. A short promise 6 once hid inside a later [ 6, 28 ], and that is why the rule on spellings exists. This book's own judge is a copy of the same grammar.

The court of perception

The record's sentence is that a comparison proves sameness, and that it never proves rightness. The library holds the case. A bar plot drew vertical bars for horizontal data while all of its seventy-three examples went on passing. This is why the plots now compare the picture exactly. That makes sameness strict; it does not make it rightness. Rightness is a person.

So a declared world carries its perception state. Eight musical traditions are declared as data in the library. Seven of them are unperceived. One was heard, and its record carries a name, a date and a verdict:

Haro
nUnheard = 0
for cName in StzSoundUniverses()
	if StzSoundUniverseQ(cName).Listener() = "UNPERCEIVED"
		nUnheard++
	ok
next
? len(StzSoundUniverses())
#--> 8
? nUnheard
#--> 7
? left(StzSoundUniverseQ("tunisian").Listener(), 5)
#--> HEARD

ran: printed what this block promises

There are no counters in this block. The one tradition that was heard was heard by the author on 26 September 2026, through five original examples, and the record's words are that it is "far from being qualified". Which part fails, whether the tuning, the phrasing, the rhythm or the timbre, is not yet said. [AUTHOR: May the book quote those four words as yours, as the clearest recorded perception that is a refusal?]

The law is the estate's, adopted on 25 September 2026 at the author's instruction, and written by a session. It requires that the record names the perceiver and quotes the verdict. Its second line is the one I take with me: unperceived is a state, not a failure. It refuses two things as well. It does not say that a human must gate every commit, because it binds at the granularity of a phase. And it does not say that it generalises from one plane without further evidence, and it was held for a month on that account.

The gallery of pictures is where it is unmet. The library holds ninety-five judgements of pictures and text sections, in three index files, committed on 5 October 2026. Every one is by a model, reading the picture or reading the text the program printed. None has a human name. The first index says it in a sentence: no human has looked at these pictures. The register of findings ends with a line I repeat: a human verdict on a sample is still owed. [AUTHOR: Is there a human verdict on any gallery picture since 5 October? If so, give the name, the date and your words, and the chapter prints them. If not, it stays "unperceived".]

The court of security

The security plane starts from a claim. The threat model assumes that a hijacked language model will get through, and makes it harmless. The model never holds the capability, and so an LLM that is fooled still cannot act. The document does not try to detect every malicious prompt.

The evidence of what happened is a hash chain. Edit one line, and the chain says which entry broke. A wrong key and an edited line are two different accusations:

Haro
oLed = StzSecurityLedger(256)
oLed.Record(StzSecurityRefusal("auth.login.failed", HumanActor("admin"), "user:admin", "wrong credentials"))
oLed.Record(StzSecurityRefusal("secret.reveal.refused", LLMActor("advisor"), "secret:payments-key", "actor is not effectful"))
oLed.SealTo("evidence.txt", "the-evidence-key")
? StzVerifySealedLedger("evidence.txt", "the-evidence-key")[:why]
#--> chain intact over 2 entries
? StzVerifySealedLedger("evidence.txt", "another-key")[:why]
#--> the chain is intact but the SEAL does not match this key
write("evidence.txt", StzReplace(read("evidence.txt"), "actor is not effectful", "routine maintenance"))
? StzVerifySealedLedger("evidence.txt", "the-evidence-key")[:why]
#--> the chain breaks at entry 2 -- that record (or one before it) was edited
remove("evidence.txt")

ran: printed what this block promises

this block touches files; the output shown was recorded on 2026-10-09 02:30 UTC+01:00

Notice what I chose as the reason to edit. A reason written as "bad password" is redacted when the record is built, so editing it leaves the chain intact. The redaction is itself a guarantee, and it hid my first attempt. The narration states the limit in its own words: this is not protection against an attacker already running code in the process.

A secret is the same law applied to a key. Its only public face is its descriptor. A hand that may commit can read it. A language model cannot, and the refusal goes into the ledger without anyone calling the ledger:

Haro
StzOpenSecurityLedger(64)
oKey = new stzSecret("deploy-key")
oKey.FromLiteralQ("ssh-ed25519-AAAA")
? oKey.Descriptor()
#--> <secret 'deploy-key' (secret) from literal>
? oKey.Reveal(HumanActor("ops"))
#--> ssh-ed25519-AAAA
try
	oKey.Reveal(LLMActor("planner"))
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> Refused: actor 'planner' (posture sandboxed) may not reveal secret 'deploy-key'. Only an effectful, non-sandboxed actor can read a secret.
? len(StzSecurityLedgerQ().Refusals())
#--> 1
StzCloseSecurityLedger()

ran: printed what this block promises

This is chapter 17's law, that a model does not hold the capability to produce effects, applied to a key, with the record added.

What does the table of guarantees tie to a guard? The meta-guard of the threat model checks that the document exists with its sections; that every guarantee row contains a proof, which is a guard's path, a fuzz run, a bill-of-materials check or a runbook; that every guard path in the rows exists on disk; and that a planted fake row with an unproven guarantee is caught. It does not run the guards, and it does not check that a guard asserts what its row says. That is the security gate's job. So "each tied to a guard" is, exactly, "each names at least one proof, and every guard file it names exists".

At this commit the table holds 43 guarantees. The site says 38, on three pages. Both are true of their dates: the document had 38 rows on 30 September 2026 at nine in the morning, and the rows from 39 to 43 were added on 5 October, the last at 16:31. The site's number is the site's to update.

The court of performance

An instrument owes a number. The honest stopwatch gives a number from a clock that only moves forward, excludes a pause, and ships two spans of one trace in one batch for an observability collector:

Haro
w = StzStopwatchXT("import-orders")
w.Lap("parsed")
w.Pause()
StzEngineTimeSleepMs(200)
w.Resume()
w.Stop()
? isnumber(w.ElapsedMs())
#--> 1
? w.ElapsedMs() < 200
#--> 1
? w.Record()[:running]
#--> 0
w2 = StzStopwatchXT("notify-customer")
w2.JoinTrace(w.TraceParent())
w2.Stop()
? w2.TraceId() = w.TraceId()
#--> 1
oBatch = StzOtelBatch("shop")
oBatch.AddSpan(w).AddSpan(w2)
? Q(oBatch.ToJson()).NumberOfOccurrence(w.TraceId())
#--> 2

ran: printed what this block promises

Careful with what this does not claim. The narration says the joined stopwatch gets a new span. I checked: it gets the same trace and the same span identifier. The sentence holds for the server's echo, which I did not run, and not for the stopwatch. I list it among the requests.

The instrument is not the end of the court. Judgment and action live inside the program. A performance plan is proposed by a machine, and only an effectful actor commits it. The same action is judged twice, and both judgments stay in the audit:

Haro
oPlan = StzPerfPlan("relieve-queue")
oPlan.Propose(:ScaleUp, "nlp", "queue.depth: measured 900 (must be <= 100)")
oFleet = new FakeFleet
? oPlan.MayCommit(LLMActor("advisor"))
#--> 0
? oPlan.ExecuteOn(oFleet, LLMActor("advisor"))
#--> 0
? oFleet.CallCount()
#--> 0
? oPlan.ExecuteOn(oFleet, HumanActor("mansour"))
#--> 1
? oFleet.CallCount()
#--> 1
oPlan.Show()
#--> Perf plan relieve-queue -- 1 proposed action(s).
#      1. scaleup 'nlp' -- queue.depth: measured 900 (must be <= 100)
#    Audit (2):
#      #1 REFUSED scaleup 'nlp' by advisor -- actor is not effectful -- expression is free; admission is governed
#      #1 COMMITTED scaleup 'nlp' by mansour -- queue.depth: measured 900 (must be <= 100)

class FakeFleet
	aFleetCalls = []
	def ScaleUp(pcTag)
		aFleetCalls + [ "scaleup", pcTag ]
	def CallCount()
		return len(aFleetCalls)

The fleet here is a rehearsal double, any object that answers the same effectful verbs. The loop is proved against the double and not against a real fleet. A model asking to commit is refused before any attempt, and the double counts zero calls.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused the word for the thing it was not. The structure of this book and the closing assessment of the study call the articles "narrations that cannot lie". My own ruling of 7 October 2026, the study's 12.20, says that "narration" names the articles under the library's documentation folder, and not the executable suites. The site's runner annotates an article and no longer decides whether it is shown. The site's own record of 8 October 2026, run on a later commit than this book's, says that of 135 articles 55 ran, and of the 423 blocks in those, 123 kept their promise. So the articles can drift. What cannot lie are the executable guards, and this book's own build, which fails when a block does not keep its promise. [AUTHOR: May the chapter say that, or do you want it to defend the older phrase?]

I refused a second assertion library. The promise runner's rulings refuse a second library, a rewrite of the test files, a coverage percentage before there are routes, the word "verified" on a perceptual claim without a name and a sentence, and a mock written for a platform's production.

I refused to fold unjudged or unperceived into pass or fail. A stop has five states and no sixth. A runner that folds the fourth or the fifth into either of the others is wrong.

I refused to analyse tampered evidence. A tool that verifies, warns, and then analyses anyway teaches its users to ignore the warning.

I refused to detect everything. Detections are declared. The sentinel speaks on transitions only: quiet, one alarm after five wrong passwords, and nothing new after a sixth, since the story did not restart. It does not write its own firings into the ledger, because detections over detection events invite feedback loops.

I refused to compete with the field's ecosystem. The performance study of 29 July 2026 says the plane does not compete with Grafana, Datadog or the ecosystem of OpenTelemetry, and should not pretend to. It exports.

I refused a guarantee without a guard. The threat model's last rule is that a guarantee is added only together with its guard.

5. The court

testoor_promises_narrated proves each promise rule planted both ways: a lie is diverged; two lies are both caught; a short lie does not hide in a later list; the spellings of a true value are all kept; an expected raise is honoured; prose is unjudged; a program that does not compile is not diverged; a raise part-way leaves the later promises unreached. threat_model_narrated proves the meta-guard described above, including its negative sibling. security_ledger_narrated, secretstore_narrated and secret_narrated prove the chain and the seal, the store and the secret. security_sentinel_narrated proves the edge-triggered sentinel. stopwatch_narrated and tracing_tail_narrated prove the instrument and the batch. governed_loop_narrated proves the plan, the preflight, the commit and the audit.

I ran threat_model_narrated alone on 8 October 2026, and it passed all of its assertions. The others are counted by the build and not run here. The performance plane has twelve guards. I do not print their sum, because the build counts them.
