6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in storage, in queries and in ecosystem. The library's own study of the performance field, written against the tools of early 2026, says it without softening: no time-series database, no query language for it, no dashboards, by design; export instead. What it claims against them is one thing: nothing in the field couples a budget to the codebase's own rule system.

The field leads in the browser. The restaurant's worlds run in the browsers of customers and the kitchen, and I found nothing in the library that measures a first display or a tap there. The library's monitor observes a server, and the SLA judges whatever numbers are recorded into a timer. The owner's measurement protocol, at the seventy-fifth percentile on a mid-range phone, cannot be declared exactly in the library's terms, which offer the fiftieth, the ninety-fifth and the ninety-ninth.

The field leads on real services. A double is not the service, and the plan says so: you still need at least one real run before production, and recorded responses drift. The real providers lead in the edge cases the sandbox does not model.

And the super-app hosts lead in installed base. The design names what the industry's super-app has, a store, a review, a native bridge, and replaces it; it does not claim users.

7. The limit

  • builtthe constellation of worlds with its bonds and norms; the payments sandbox and the delivery gate that refuses a fake; the speed budget declared and judged
  • designedthe Lock as a rule of the library; the constellation written in the near-natural idiom the design describes; a speed expectation in the owner's own percentile; browser-side timing
  • absentthe restaurant's live payment adapter; a measurement of the budget on a real mobile network; the platform on the Softanza engine

What is built: the constellation of worlds with its bonds and norm-gated crossings, retirement, revival, hot swap and nesting; the payments sandbox and the delivery gate; the speed budget declared and judged; the graph rules the Lock's construction uses.

What is designed: the Lock as a rule of the library, of which the record has no code; the near-natural idiom of the constellation, with the verbs the design names and the class does not have; the two-gesture rule and the other interface rules as checks; a seventy-fifth percentile expectation; browser-side timing.

What is absent: the restaurant's live payment adapter, which the library's charter calls a later task and the owner's decision; a measurement of the budget on a real mobile network, which the project's dashboard of 23 August postponed to the next cycle; and the state of the platform after 25 August 2026, where the record ends. Nothing in it says the first version reached production at the restaurant, passed the go-live gate, or took a real order from a real customer. [AUTHOR: What happened after 25 August 2026? And may the book print the owner's tightened speed thresholds and his measurement protocol, or only say that such a budget exists?]

And what runs today is ordinary. The worlds are single HTML files, one per world, with a vendored framework, no build step and no content network. The server is a Node program of a few hundred lines that uses five of Node's own modules, serves the worlds on the local network, and keeps one thing: a journal, chained by hashes, replayed at restart. The first management application has a phone wrapper around a web view. None of it runs on the Softanza engine. The library is the project's design reference and the origin, in the project's own account, of its service, delivery and performance planes. The constellation is, in the site's words, a design the library can run. The restaurant does not.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerYou declare worlds and bonds and run a constellation in which a call to a world that is not yet active is refused with its reason. The restaurant's own code, however, is a web application.
The analystRigour in numbers was the contract of the first application: a due date computed from the invoice date, a date required, a debt with no due date made visible.
The designerFifteen interface rules from one directive, the three-second test; and a refused button is disabled and visible, never hidden. [AUTHOR: Who held the phone in the eleven iterations, the owner or you? The project's files say the real user, and they say you; the sentence needs one answer.]
The decision-makerThe owner accepted the Lock in writing, tightened the speed budget himself, and kept the gate on fixed fees. The library's mirror is a deployment that an entitled person may commit and that is still refused over a fake.
The educatorThe record supports only a small thing: the first application taught its user by doing, with guides whose words leave no doubt. There is no educator in this story, and I say so.
The agentAn agent can drive a production deployment and change nothing: the gate passes the services, nothing is committed, and the reason given is the actor and not the services. In the project, the agent is the session working beside me under the Lock, with a person deciding.

Declare your own Lock for one cycle. Write the worlds of the cycle you are in, three of them, as a restaurant would: the customer's phone, the kitchen screen, and one more, each with the written reason it is in. Add a fourth, the idea you had this morning. Run the court. Change the declaration, not the court, until it says the cycle is sound.

#--> 1

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

The court will tell you the circumstance and the rule. It will not write the declaration. If you want a harder one, add a rule about the actions of your cycle, and find the action that costs a third gesture.

Part VI · Chapter 29

A bank in Niamey

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-09 02:33 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 6 of 6 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

A bank is judged on its structure as much as on its numbers. A regulator asks who reports to whom: whether the audit function is independent of the executives it audits, whether there is a board, whether a risk function exists, whether the person who operates a payment is the one who approves it. The field answers with documents: an organisation chart drawn in a slide, a policy written in a word processor, an audit that compares the two once a year.

The field also has a family of tools called governance, risk and compliance platforms, which keep registers of risks and controls and track findings through to closure. They record that a control exists and who owns it. They do not read the structure of the organisation and tell you that it is wrong. (General knowledge, not a study of the record.)

2. The first principle

An organisation can be judged by its own chart, under a regulator's rules, by a program that reads the chart as data: the chart says what is, the rule says what must be, and the verdict names the rule and the place.

3. The Softanza form

A commercial bank in Niamey, under the rules of the central bank of the West African monetary union, runs an organisation-assessment product I built. It is installed on the bank's own internal network, under licence, and the installation guide I delivered to the bank is the document that attests the reference. The product itself is a Python application: a small web server with a database. I say that first, because the lesson I am going to show you is in the library, and not inside that product.

The lesson is that an organisation chart is data a program can judge. It begins with a text that a person can edit, with no programming: positions, their titles, their departments, and who each one reports to. This is the chart of a small bank:

Haro
cChart = '
orgchart "bank"

positions
    board
        title: Board of Directors
        level: executive
        department: board
        reportsTo:

    ceo
        title: Chief Executive
        level: executive
        department: executive
        reportsTo: board

    risk
        title: Chief Risk Officer
        level: management
        department: risk
        reportsTo: board

    audit
        title: Internal Audit
        level: management
        department: audit
        reportsTo: ceo
'
oOrg = new stzOrgChart("bank")
oOrg.ImportStzOrg(cChart)
? oOrg.NodeCount()
#--> 4
? @@( oOrg.ValidateXT(:BCEAO)[:issues] )
#--> [ "BCEAO-002: Audit reports to non-board position" ]
? oOrg.IsValidXT(:BCEAO)
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

The regulator's rule reads the chart. Audit reports to the chief executive, and the verdict says so, with a rule code an auditor can look up. A chart is judged by more than one court at a time, each finding carries its own code, and the compliance report says compliant or not. Here a second rule, the segregation of duties, which says operations must not report to treasury:

Haro
oOrg.AddManagementPositionXT("treasury", "Treasury")
oOrg.SetPositionDepartment("treasury", "treasury")
oOrg.AddManagementPositionXT("ops", "Operations")
oOrg.SetPositionDepartment("ops", "operations")
oOrg.ReportsTo("treasury", "ceo")
oOrg.ReportsTo("ops", "treasury")
aV = oOrg.ValidateXT([ :BCEAO, :SOD ])
? aV[:validatorsFailed]
#--> 2
? aV[:results][1][:issues][1]
#--> BCEAO-002: Audit reports to non-board position
? aV[:results][2][:issues][1]
#--> SOD-001: Operations reports through Treasury
? oOrg.ComplianceReport()[:overallStatus]
#--> non-compliant

ran: printed what this block promises

The library names seven regimes: the regional one, Basel III, SOX, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, GDPR and HIPAA. They share one mechanism. I will print what each holds, rather than write a sentence that says "Basel III is validated":

Haro
aBases = [ new stzBCEAORuleBase(), new stzBaselIIIRuleBase(), new stzSOXRuleBase(), new stzPCIDSSRuleBase(),
           new stzISO27001RuleBase(), new stzGDPRRuleBase(), new stzHIPAARuleBase() ]
for oBase in aBases
	? oBase.Name() + " : " + oBase.NumberOfRules()
next
#--> BCEAO : 4
#--> Basel III : 4
#--> SOX : 5
#--> PCI-DSS : 4
#--> ISO 27001 : 4
#--> GDPR : 4
#--> HIPAA : 4

ran: printed what this block promises

Four rules every base carries: nobody reports to themselves, no reporting cycle, no orphan position, and a span of control. SOX adds one of its own, the separation of duties. The library's comment says it plainly: the regime classes differ by name today, and only one adds a rule of its own. I will come back to what that means.

A bank's own rule is data too. Take the rule that internal audit reports to the board. It is not code. It names the department it governs, the line it requires and the sentence it prints, and it is added to a regime's rule base. The report says which rule broke, and where:

Haro
oRule = new stzGraphRule("audit-reports-to-board")
oRule.SetDomainQ("orgchart")
oRule.WhenQ("department", "equals", "audit")
oRule.ThenQ("reportsTo", "equals", "board")
oRule.ThenViolationQ("internal audit must report to the board")
oBasel = new stzBaselIIIRuleBase()
oBasel.AddRule(oRule)
oRep = new stzRuleReport("bank")
oRep.Ingest(oOrg.CheckCompliance(oBasel))
oRep.Report()
#--> Rule report 'bank': 1 finding(s), 1 error(s), 0 warning(s) -> UNSOUND (errors present)
#      [orgchart] 1 finding(s)
#        ERROR audit-reports-to-board @ audit -- internal audit must report to the board

ran: printed what this block promises

Then the verdict follows the chart. Two edits to two reporting lines, audit now to the board and operations to the chief executive, and the courts that said no say yes:

Haro
oOrg.ReportsTo("audit", "board")
oOrg.ReportsTo("ops", "ceo")
? oOrg.IsValidXT([ :BCEAO, :SOD ])
#--> 1
? oOrg.ComplianceReport()[:overallStatus]
#--> compliant
oRep = new stzRuleReport("bank")
oRep.Ingest(oOrg.CheckCompliance(oBasel))
oRep.Report()
#--> Rule report 'bank': 0 finding(s), 0 error(s), 0 warning(s) -> SOUND
? oRep.IsSound()
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

That is the move the narration of a virtual bank tells, from a non-compliant structure to a governed one, and the report is one gate over every court. And here is the limit of it, as a block. A court reads what the chart declares and no more. Leave the chief executive's department blank, and an audit function that reports to him passes; declare the department and the finding appears:

Haro
oOrg2 = new stzOrgChart("bank")
oOrg2.ImportStzOrg( substr(cChart, "department: executive", "department:") )
? oOrg2.IsValidXT(:BCEAO)
#--> 1
? oOrg2.ValidateXT(:Banking)[:status]
#--> pass
oOrg2.SetPositionDepartment("ceo", "executive")
? oOrg2.IsValidXT(:BCEAO)
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

The same block shows that the banking validator always passes: it is, in the library's own words, a placeholder for rules not written yet.

My first book, Refinement-Oriented Programming, tells the discipline of governing change through the story of a bank facing a regulator's letter. This chapter does not retell it. It tells what the library carries.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused to hide the structure in a database. In the delivered product, an organisation chart is rows in two tables. In the library, it is a text that a person can read and edit, and the same text is the unit the court judges. A rule applied to a database row is a query; a rule applied to a text is something a person can read before it runs.

I refused to claim more than the library holds. The Forged page of the site uses the word "validator" for two different things. The regional regulator has a validator of three rules, and a rule base of four universal ones. Basel III has the rule base only, and so do the others. I printed the count, and the block above shows it.

I refused to carry a regulator's text in a code I cannot source. The codes BCEAO-001 to BCEAO-003 are the library's own; the record ties them to no article of the central bank's text. [AUTHOR: Which text of the central bank are BCEAO-001 to BCEAO-003 drawn from? The book should say, or say that they are the library's own.]

I refused to tell what I do not know. What the bank's own people declare, operate or say is not in the record. The installation guide is my document to the bank: installation steps, a licence file, a support contact. The Forged page keeps no figure and no person of a client. The record is silent on who at the bank declares the chart, how long the product has been installed, and how many people use it. I will invent none of it. [AUTHOR: Who at the bank declares the chart, the questionnaire or the rules, and in what sense is the delivered product "built with Softanza"? Chapter 1 says it is, and the record shows a Python application that calls nothing of the library.]

5. The court

orgrule_narrated proves the seven rule bases as one mechanism over the chart's graph, with the four universal rules and the separation of duties that SOX adds. 14_bceao_governance proves the regional validator. 15_multiple_validators proves the combined verdict, and 13_segregation_of_duties the second court. rulereport_narrated proves the one report over every court. 36_import_from_stzorg proves the text form of the chart.

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in coverage. A governance and compliance platform holds a register of every regulation, every control and every finding, with workflows, owners and deadlines. The library holds one structural check of a regional regulator, one of segregation of duties, and a mechanism. For GDPR, HIPAA and the others, it holds the mechanism and the four universal rules, and nothing that is specific to them.

The field leads in actual use: a platform that a bank's auditors already know, and that a regulator has already seen.

Where I think this stands apart is that the chart is the data and the court is a rule over it. A chart is a text, a rule is data, a finding names the rule and the position, and the report is one verdict. The library's own comparison table for this feature is all wins, undated, with cost figures that cite nothing, and I will not print it.

7. The limit

  • builtthe organisation chart as a text a person can edit; the validators of the regional regulator and of segregation of duties; the seven regimes as one mechanism; a rule written as data; one report with one verdict
  • designedthe content that would make the other six regimes differ from the first; a rule file that judges, and not only loads
  • absentthe delivered product running on the library; a word from the bank's own people; an auditor's reading of a finding the library produced

What is built: the organisation chart as a model and as text; the validators of the regional regulator and of segregation of duties; the seven regimes as one mechanism with the SOX exemplar; a rule written as data; the one report with its verdict.

What is designed, or built in part:

  • The content of the six other regimes. Each holds the same four universal rules.
  • A rule file that judges. The library can load a file of rules in a when and then text, and the one in its test data loads two rules. After the load, on a chart with no board and an audit position under the chief executive, the report said sound. The format is admitted, and the rule is not enforced.
  • A validator reads declared properties. It finds the board by the word "board" in a position title, and it needs the departments to be declared.
  • The succession validator flags every filled position, by the library's own comment a known defect. The reorganisation simulation raises when it is asked to change a reporting line, also a known defect. The article that tells the simulation names a method that exists nowhere in the library.

What is absent:

  • The delivered product running on the library. It is a Python application; a search of its code found no regional or Basel check and no call to the library.
  • A word from the bank. The record is silent.
  • A perceived verdict. No document says that an auditor or a supervisor read a finding that the library produced.
  • A delivery date. The delivered files carry file-system times, and those are not a delivery date.

The web layer of the product was born in its own repository: its first commit is dated 4 February 2026, and the interface constitution's text was first committed on 8 February. The constitution's rules 117 to 124 were harvested from a banking-supervision product, in the record's words, and the record does not say that product is the bank's installation. I will not say that it is.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerThe chart is a text, the rule is data, the court is a call. A finding names the rule and the position.
The analystYou change a reporting line in a text and you re-run: the verdict follows the chart.
The designerThe report is one verdict over every court: sound or unsound, with each finding where it was found.
The decision-makerAsk which of the regulations the library holds, and ask for the count. Seven regimes, one with real content of its own and one that adds a rule; the rest carry the universal four.
The educatorThe narration of a virtual bank tells the move from a non-compliant structure to a governed one, and the book shows the move with calls that run.
The agentYou may read a chart and a report. A rule you add is data a person can read, and the court judges the chart with it.

Then write a rule of your own as data, one that governs one department, and say what the report will print.

Run it. Then leave one department blank and say which finding disappears, and why that is dangerous.

An organisation in the field

Draft · not yet read by the author

1. The concept, as the field holds it

The field has two practices that this project needed, and keeps them in separate places.

The first is the business rule that a business person can change. Rule engines and decision tables have existed for decades; the Decision Model and Notation, a standard of 2015, gives business analysts a table in which an approval ceiling is a number in a cell. The second is the application that keeps working with no network. Offline-first design is a practice of its own, with synchronising databases and, since an essay of 2019, a name for its philosophy, local-first software: the data is on your device, and the network is a convenience.

A third practice has come with the agents: a model proposes, and a person approves. In the field it is a button.

2. The first principle

The organisation's own study of the project says it in one sentence, and I take it as the principle of this chapter: the agent proposes, and a person decides.

3. The Softanza form

An organisation works in Niger, with a head office in Niamey and bases in the field. Its own specification preferred a low-code platform built on a large vendor's office suite. My offer of 5 August 2026 was the one retained, for a reason chapter 2 gave: ownership. It owns its vocabulary and its rules; it changes them without programming; it pays no licence per seat; and it can hand everything to a developer of its own country. We built the design study together, with its teams, from 22 September to 8 October 2026. I say "design study" and not "delivery" every time, because the hub is not built. The study's version 1.2 is submitted to the executive director for validation, and the record does not say it was validated.

Four things in that study the library carries. I will show them in the order the organisation would meet them, and then the one it asked for that the library does not carry.

A rule is data. An approval ceiling is a sentence with a number in it, attached to the model of the advances it governs. The model judges itself, and says how many subjects the rule looks at. The data below are invented for this chapter, four advances with an amount and a count of approvals; they are not the organisation's figures, and the numbers five hundred and two hundred are mine, not its thresholds.

Haro
oG = new stzGraph("advances")
oG.AddNodeXTT("a0", "A0", [ :amount = 120, :approvals = 1 ])
oG.AddNodeXTT("a1", "A1", [ :amount = 250, :approvals = 1 ])
oG.AddNodeXTT("a2", "A2", [ :amount = 600, :approvals = 1 ])
oG.AddNodeXTT("a3", "A3", [ :amount = 900, :approvals = 2 ])
oRule = new stzGraphRule("second-approval")
oRule.SetDomainQ("advances")
oRule.SetMessageQ("above the ceiling an advance needs two approvals")
oRule.WhenQ("amount", "greaterthan", 500)
oRule.ThenQ("approvals", "greaterthan", 1)
oRule.ThenViolationQ("two approvals needed")
oG.AddRule(oRule)
oG.RulesReport()
#--> Rule report 'advances': 1 finding(s), 1 error(s), 0 warning(s) -> UNSOUND (errors present)
#      [advances] 1 finding(s)
#        ERROR second-approval @ a2 -- two approvals needed
? len(oRule.SubjectsIn(oG))
#--> 2

ran: printed what this block promises

The ceiling is changed, and the same model is judged again. A change of the rule is a change of its values, and the verdict and its scope follow:

Haro
oG.ClearAttachedRules()
oRule = new stzGraphRule("second-approval")
oRule.SetDomainQ("advances")
oRule.SetMessageQ("above the ceiling an advance needs two approvals")
oRule.WhenQ("amount", "greaterthan", 200)
oRule.ThenQ("approvals", "greaterthan", 1)
oRule.ThenViolationQ("two approvals needed")
oG.AddRule(oRule)
oG.RulesReport()
#--> Rule report 'advances': 2 finding(s), 2 error(s), 0 warning(s) -> UNSOUND (errors present)
#      [advances] 2 finding(s)
#        ERROR second-approval @ a1 -- two approvals needed
#        ERROR second-approval @ a2 -- two approvals needed
? len(oRule.SubjectsIn(oG))
#--> 3

ran: printed what this block promises

I have to be honest about what this block shows. The "change" is a rule rebuilt in code with another number. That the organisation's own person changes it like filling in a form is the study's promise, and I did not find a file of the library that makes it so; section 7 says what does and does not exist.

What the library does carry is the answer to the worst thing that can go wrong when a non-programmer edits a rule: a rule that quietly governs nothing. Misspell a property, and the rule finds nothing, and the model reports that it is sound. A governor, which asks rules what they govern and not what they say, names the dead rule:

Haro
oTypo = new stzGraphRule("second-approval-typo")
oTypo.SetMessageQ("above the ceiling an advance needs two approvals")
oTypo.WhenQ("amont", "greaterthan", 200)
oTypo.ThenQ("approvals", "greaterthan", 1)
oTypo.ThenViolationQ("two approvals needed")
? len(oTypo.Check(oG))
#--> 0
oWatch = StzRuleGovernance("hub")
oWatch.AddRule(oTypo)
oWatch.AddCase("advances", oG)
aF = oWatch.CheckRules()
? aF[1][:rule]
#--> scope_empty
? aF[1][:message]
#--> governs nothing in 1 pictures -- a dead rule and a misspelt scope predicate both report as passing
oWatch2 = StzRuleGovernance("hub")
oWatch2.AddRule(oRule)
oWatch2.AddCase("advances", oG)

A dead rule and an all-clear produce identical output: silence. The court has to tell "nothing was wrong" from "nothing was looked at". The word "pictures" in the message is the governor's origin: it was built for the graph plane's drawings first, and I would say "cases".

A person sees the refusal. When an answer breaks a law the organisation declared, it is refused with its reason, and the refusal is kept as a checkpoint for a person to see, with its context. Chapter 17 showed the asking half of this machine. Here is the refusing half: a request needs one approval, the law says a request has one approver, and a second approver is refused:

Haro
oKB = new stzKnowledgeGraph("requests")
oKB.AddConversationQ("review").SetGoal(StzGoalQ().RequireOne("request-7", "approved-by"))
? oKB.AskIn("review")
#--> What does 'request-7' have for 'approved-by'?  (why: 'request-7' needs 'approved-by')
oKB.ConstrainRelation("approved-by", :Unique)
oKB.KnowRelation("request-7", "approved-by", "approver-1")
aR = oKB.ReplyIn("review", "approver-2")
? aR[:refused][1][2]
#--> 'request-7' already bears 'approved-by' (to 'approver-1'); the relation is :Unique
aCp = oKB.ConversationQ("review").Checkpoints()
? len(aCp)
#--> 1
? aCp[1][:attempted]
#--> approver-2
? aCp[1][:why]
#--> 'request-7' already bears 'approved-by' (to 'approver-1'); the relation is :Unique

ran: printed what this block promises

Authority is not permission. The assistant of this organisation may prepare a file. It may hold the permission to release an advance and still be refused, because its authority does not cover the act's risk. A person with the authority is allowed. The verdict says why, in either case:

Haro
oGov = new stzGovernance("hub")
oGov.DeclareRisk("prepare-file", 1)
oGov.DeclareRisk("release-advance", 3)
oGov.GrantPermission("assistant", "prepare-file")
oGov.GrantPermission("assistant", "release-advance")
oGov.SetAuthority("assistant", :Advisory)
oGov.GrantPermission("approver-1", "release-advance")
oGov.SetAuthority("approver-1", :Autonomous)
? oGov.MayProceed("assistant", "prepare-file")
#--> 1
? oGov.MayProceed("assistant", "release-advance")
#--> 0
? oGov.Why()
#--> refused: 'assistant' holds 'advisory' authority (level 1) but 'release-advance' is risk tier 3 (SHOULD does not cover it)
? oGov.MayProceed("approver-1", "release-advance")
#--> 1
? oGov.Why()
#--> allowed: permission held AND 'autonomous' authority (level 3) covers risk tier 3

ran: printed what this block promises

The library knows an actor only by a name and an authority level. Whether an actor is a person or an assistant is what its level is declared to be, and binding a level to a signed-in person is the work of the authentication plane, which I have not read for this chapter.

A decision keeps its authority at the time. Each decision records its reason, its actor, the act, the authority and the risk of that moment. A new decision supersedes the old one without erasing it:

Haro
nAt = 1785700000000
oGov.RecordDecisionAt("c-1", "ceiling raised for the harvest season", "approver-1", "release-advance", nAt)
oGov.RecordDecisionAt("c-1", "ceiling restored, the season is over", "approver-1", "release-advance", nAt + 3600000)
? oGov.LineageOf("c-1")[:rationale]
#--> ceiling restored, the season is over
? len(oGov.LineageHistoryOf("c-1"))
#--> 2
? oGov.LineageHistoryOf("c-1")[1][:rationale]
#--> ceiling raised for the harvest season
? oGov.LineageOf("c-1")[:authorityAtTime]
#--> autonomous

ran: printed what this block promises

The instant is a fixed number, so the clock is not read. This keeps the decision answerable. It is not a version store for the rule itself, and I will not pretend it is.

And the one the organisation asked for first. Its default option is to work offline: bases in the field with no network, entering what they do and sending it later. The library knows offline as a declared, governed capability of a world, asked for and granted or refused like the camera or payments. That is all it knows:

Haro
oApp = StzAppQ("field-visits")
oPlat = StzPlatformQ("field")
oPlat.SetWorld(oApp)
oRegime = new stzGovernance("field-regime")
oRegime.GrantPermission("field-visits", "use-offline")
oRegime.SetAuthority("field-visits", :Advisory)
oPlat.SetGovernedBy(oRegime)
? oPlat.Granted(:offline)
#--> 0
? oPlat.Why()
#--> capability 'offline' was never requested via AddCapabilityQ().
oPlat.AddCapabilityQ(:offline).SetPurposes([ :enter_without_network ])
? oPlat.Granted(:offline)
#--> 1
? oPlat.Why()
#--> allowed: permission held AND 'advisory' authority (level 1) covers risk tier 1

Read this block as a limit and not as a win. Nothing in it queues anything. The library does not keep entries on a device, send them when the network comes back, or settle two people's edits.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused a per-seat platform as the organisation's ground. The specification preferred low-code on a vendor's suite. The retained offer proposes Softanza for one reason above the others: the organisation owns its vocabulary and its rules, which it can change without programming, and the whole of the work, programs, configuration and data, is its own, with a handover to a local developer. The vendor's suite stays where it was good, for the user accounts, the documents and the notifications. [AUTHOR: Who chose, and what was weighed against low-code? The record has the outcome and the gains, listed without a ranking, and not the deliberation.]

I refused to let the assistant decide. It proposes. Its authority is advisory; a person's covers the risk. The refusal names the level, the risk tier, and the sentence that says the authority does not cover the act.

I refused a silent rule. A rule that governs nothing is reported. A rule with no message is reported too. That is the price of letting a non-programmer touch a rule, and I did not wait for the first incident to pay it.

I refused to call offline a lesson. The Forged page says it in four words: a gap, not a lesson. A restaurant asked for the same. The study is clear that offline is the organisation's default, and the library has only a permission for it. [AUTHOR: The organisation's study says its offline part "is already in service", and the Forged page says "a gap". The record of a sister package of the estate, a browser-side one, holds a durable outbox on the device and an ordered, idempotent replay, and I did not run it. May the book mention it, as outside the library and not run?]

5. The court

graphruleset_narrated proves a rule with a comparison and a requirement turned into an implication. gg_rule_governance proves that a rule that governs nothing is reported. wisecoding_narrated, its third scene, proves a refusal that is governed and checkpointed. governance_narrated proves that can is not should: permission held and authority lacking is a refusal. governance_lineage_narrated proves the decision kept with its authority at the time. 01_platform_narrated proves the capability seam: the camera granted, payments refused, a capability never asked for refused with an honest reason. The guard does not itself use the capability for offline; the block above does, with the tier the platform declares for it.

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in business rules for business people. Decision tables are a standard; a person edits a cell, not a program. Here the change is a rule rebuilt in code, and the file form that would carry a rule as text loads rules and judges nothing: it reads a rule's name, its kind, its severity, its function and its message, and does not read the when and then lines of its own sample.

The field leads in offline. Local-first software is a practice with synchronising databases and a decade of experience. The library has a permission.

The field leads in people. A decision table is a thing a trained analyst already knows how to read. And the organisation's own specification, which preferred the vendor's suite, had good reasons: its users already have accounts there.

7. The limit

  • builta rule written as data on a model, changed and judged again; the governor that names a rule that governs nothing; a refusal that reaches a person with its context; authority set against risk; a decision kept with its authority at the time; offline as a capability a world must ask for
  • designedthe hub and its study; a rule language a local developer can learn; the study's promises that a rule is checked before it applies and can be undone
  • absentthe hub, built; a mechanism for work done offline, kept and sent later; a version history of a rule; a customer platform on the engine

What is built: a rule as data, changed and judged again; the governor that names a dead rule; the checkpoint; authority against risk; the lineage; offline as a capability.

What is designed: the hub and its study, whose schedule is in the future; a rule language that a local developer can learn, whose sample in the study is written in a notation that is not the library's; and the study's promises about rules: that they are checked before they apply, that their effect is shown before it is applied, that they can be undone and that their history is kept. The library has the pieces, the governor, the refusal of an unknown rule type or a missing file, and the refusal of a duplicate name.

What is absent: a version history of a rule with an undo: the lineage records the decision, and the rule is rebound; I found no store of rule versions, and my search was not exhaustive. The hub, built. Offline as a mechanism: no class in the library queues, synchronises or settles a conflict. And a customer platform on the Softanza engine.

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerA rule is an object with a comparison and a requirement, attached to a model, and a governor tells you when it governs nothing.
The analystYou change a rule's values, not its program, and the model is judged again with the new scope.
The designerA refusal keeps its context for the person who will read it.
The decision-makerAuthority is not permission: ask which level covers which risk, and read the lineage of a decision.
The educatorAn organisation's rule can be taught as a sentence with a number in it.
The agentYou prepare. A person decides. And you will be refused, with the level and the risk tier named.

9. Exercise

Pick one rule of an organisation you know that has a number in it, a ceiling, a delay, a count of approvals. Write it as a rule with a condition and a requirement, on four invented cases, two that satisfy it and two that do not. Before you run anything, write the report you expect. Then misspell one property of the condition on purpose, and say what the model reports, and what the governor reports.

Run it. The difference between those two answers is the chapter.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

The field has three habits for saying what a piece of work has proved.

The first is the reference: a logo on a home page, a customer story of two pages, the sentence "trusted by". It proves that someone paid or signed. It does not say what they ran, for how long, or what they said.

The second is the readiness scale. NASA's technology readiness levels, later an international standard, name how far a technology has travelled from a laboratory to the place it was built for. The highest level is a system proven in operation. It is a vocabulary of stage, and this book uses one of its own (built, designed, absent).

The third is the limits section. An empirical study must state its threats to validity; a machine-learning model ships with a card whose last part is its caveats; an artifact submitted to a research conference is badged by what someone else did with it. This is the form closest to this chapter, and the one most often skipped when the reader is a buyer.

What the three have in common is that the claim and its proof travel apart. A page says "used by", and the proof is a trust in the page. (General knowledge, not a study of the record.)

2. The first principle

The record gives two sentences, and they are one. The site says: "Nothing is a reference until a document proves it." And, of what the author remembers: what "no file proves is not listed."

A project proves exactly what a document, a file, a run and a named person reach, and the page says where they stop. [AUTHOR: Is this the principle in your words, or the site's two sentences as they stand?]

3. The Softanza form

This chapter is the other half of chapters 28 to 30. Those told what three projects taught the library. This one says, project by project, what they did not prove. I did not write it after the fact, to be modest. The site carries the same page, with the same heading, and it was written before any reader asked.

The shape of the answer is a table of three columns for each project: the claim, the document or file that proves it, and what is absent. I leave a cell empty when I cannot name what fills it. And I will not fill the third column from memory.

Before the tables, five small blocks. Each is a place where the library shows an absence by refusing, instead of passing silently. They are the chapter's sentence, written as code.

A dependency declared and never bound is an error. The surface of a solution is declared before anything is bound. What a rehearsal can claim, and what only the target can. The platform model gives three verdicts for the same operation. Refused: the target forbids it. Native: the host can really do it. Rehearsed: the target allows it and the host lacks it, so the run proves only the plan. Reading a pin on a development machine is rehearsed and never native. The word depends on the machine this book was run on: a Windows PC has no such pin, and a board that has one would print native for the same line.

oSol.DevelopedOn(:Windows)
oSol.WithServer(:backend, :LinuxServer)
oSol.WithApp(:firmware, :ESP32)

? oFw.ReadPin(4)
#--> rehearsed
try
	oFw.Spawn("worker")
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> scope 'esp32' (espidf) forbids 'process' -- spawn 'worker'. This target has no such capability.
oFw.Show()
#--> Scope: esp32 (espidf)
#      [rehearsed] read pin 4

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused the author's memory as evidence. The site lists nothing that I remember and no file proves. The same rule bound the bank: I know the product, because I built it, and what the bank's own people did with it is not in a file.

I refused to call the library the origin of what it only uses as an example. The forged page says "example" where the library holds a project as its example and not as its origin. And I will not repeat a sentence in the study of 12.29 that says a lesson was "born of the client's need". The registry and the SLA were first committed after the reversal of 4 July, and the order of the commits makes "born of" unproved. What I can say is "needed" and "carries".

I refused two wordings of my own. In chapters 1, 2 and 33 I wrote that the bank "runs" a product "built with" Softanza, and that the restaurant "runs" a platform. The record shows a Python application that does not call the library, built beside it by the same person, and for the restaurant a first delivery and a field day, then silence after 25 August. The honest wording is built by me, under the discipline the library now carries, and delivered and field-tested. [AUTHOR: May I correct chapters 1, 2 and 33 to those wordings? Chapter 1 is your text, and I have changed none of it.]

I refused a stage word the repository does not carry. The site's estate page says it: never called available before it is. A piece of work that reaches a person through a sense is perceived by a person, and until then it is unperceived, which is a state and not a failure.

I refused to print a percentage. I have said aloud how far the bridge runtime has come. The study ruled that the figure should not be printed without the guard that produces it. I agree.

5. The court

service_registry_narrated proves that a declared service nobody backs is an error finding, that an unbound service raises, and that a sandbox in production is a violation. full_scope_model_narrated, scenes 5 to 8, proves the three verdicts: refused, rehearsed, native. payments_live_adapter_narrated proves the adapter against a twin served over HTTP, an adapter without credentials that refuses to guess, and the scenario that says stage (b) is unperceived. It starts real server processes, and the book does not run it; it only counts its assertions. sound_mu5_narrated proves, in its fifth scene, that while the verdict is unperceived Sing returns nothing and says why. deployment_narrated proves that an undersized host is not feasible, and that an assistant rehearses and commits nothing; it writes a scratch folder beside itself, so the book does not run it either. orgrule_narrated and governance_narrated carry the other two lessons.

The court of this chapter's subject is not a guard. It is a line of the record, of the form the estate's law prescribes: a date, a person, and what they said. The library holds one such line in its data, in the sound plane. The estate holds one in its record, and chapter 33 tells it.

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in production. Ordinary stacks run real workloads for real users, including, on the site's own page, the three platforms of this part.

The field leads in references at scale. The site prints two references and a design study, and quotes no number of countries and no number of developers. A buyer reading a logo wall sees more.

The field leads in live infrastructure. Provisioning tools drive real providers every day. The library's deployment stops short of a real host, and the fifth block shows where.

The field leads in hardware in the field. The declared machine boots and judges itself in an emulator, and the vision says no customer runs on it. Its guarantee text says four of four promised, three kept in the emulator; the fourth, surviving a cut, waits for a watchdog on a real board, and the board is on order.

The field leads in speed. The runtime Softanza measured itself against was faster on every row, by a factor between one and two, and both benchmarks were run on the former runtime.

The field leads in pictures judged by people. Forty-one pictures and text sections of the gallery were judged by a model: twenty right, nine wrong, twelve uncertain. The record says that no human has looked at them.

Where I think the record stands apart is that its limit is a page, with a heading, written before any reader asked. Every stage has a word. A feature can be built and still refuse until a named person has spoken. And a live run that could not happen is reported unperceived, never a failure and never a pass.

7. The limit

  • builtthe three lessons the library carries, each with a guard (a fake never ships; a chart judged under a regulator's rules; authority against risk, with its lineage); refusals that show an absence instead of hiding it
  • designedthe customers' declarations written as Softanza's own; the five-row guarantee sheet; a runtime that is the language's own running the library; the declared machine on a board
  • absentany customer platform on the engine; a word from the bank; the restaurant's use after 25 August 2026; the hub; an offline mechanism in the library; a live payments run against the hub's sandbox; a named person's verdict on any of it

This whole chapter is a limit. Here is its sum in the stage words.

What is built: the three lessons that are proved. A fake never ships: the registry and the delivery gate. An organisation is judged by its own chart under a regulator's rules: the organisation chart and its validators. Authority is not permission, and a decision keeps its authority at the time: the governance object. Each has a file of the library that carries it, a guard that resolves, and a block already kept in a neighbouring chapter. The limit of each is in the tables: a sandbox is bound and no live payment adapter is; the bank's product does not call the chart validator; no hub exists and offline is a gap.

What is designed: the customers' declarations written as Softanza's own; the five-row guarantee sheet; the runtime that is the language's own, running the library; the declared machine on a board.

What is absent: any customer platform on the engine; a word from the bank; the restaurant's use after 25 August; the hub; an offline mechanism in the library; a live payments run against the hub's sandbox; a named person's verdict on any of it.

The sum of every absent cell is the one line chapter 33 says is still owed: the solution ran on Softanza's own engine, and this is what the user said. 8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerYour demo is a rehearsal until a target has run it. Ask the scope whether the line was native, rehearsed or refused, and write the same word beside your own claims.
The analystWhen you cite a project, write three columns: the claim, the document, and what is absent. Do not fill the third from memory.

The decision-makerRead the stage word before the testimonial. "Built" is a statement about a guard. "Runs at a customer" is a statement about a document, and you can ask for it in writing, with a name beside it.
The educatorTeach the difference between a project that taught the library and a project that runs on it. The first is proved here, and the second is the line still owed. Unperceived is a state, not a failure.
The agentYou may read the tables and quote any cell. You may not turn an absent cell into a present one. If you do, the next reader of the record will find your sentence and the missing file side by side.

Part VII · Chapter 32Spine

Many minds on one body of work

Draft · not yet read by the author

Run on 2026-10-09 02:34 UTC+01:00 inside the library at commit 93d7a39bd: 3 of 3 blocks kept their promise.

The blocks were run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27; Haro does not run the library yet. The engine binaries were built in a checkout of this commit, newest built 2026-10-05 20:27 UTC+01:00; 1 engine change(s) committed after that build are not in them.

1. The concept, as the field holds it

When the field speaks of many agents working on one body of code, it usually means a framework. A program holds several agents, a supervisor routes messages between them, and the coordination is a feature of that program. Microsoft's AutoGen, CrewAI and LangChain's LangGraph are the names you will meet, all from the last three years.

When the field speaks of the rules those agents follow, it means a file the agent reads when it starts, a page of instructions in the repository. And when it speaks of many writers on one repository, it means what teams have always used: branches, review, hooks that run before a commit, a list of who owns which folder. These are good tools, and I use them every day.

2. The first principle

The one sentence this part of the record returns to was written by one of the sessions, and I keep it because it is right: every law cites the incident that earned it; a law without a dated failure behind it is a preference.

3. The Softanza form

Softanza was not written by one hand for long. For the last two years, most of its new code has been written by sessions of a model, many at a time, on one machine, in some twenty repositories that depend on each other. I rule; they propose, build, measure and report. The record calls me the Principal. In this chapter I will simply say I.

There is no framework here. No supervisor, no broker, no graph of agents. The arrangement is files and a version history. One repository, the central one, holds the protocol: how a session reports, how it asks, how it closes. Each repository has a mailbox. Each session writes its messages in one fixed form, eight keys in a fixed order, which you have already met if you read the memos at the end of each phase of this book: by whom, about what, why, what was done, the state of named things, what is waiting and on whom, what comes next, and one line of judgement. Every message is also appended to a dated file, so that the day's reasoning is never only in a chat window that closes.

What makes it a discipline and not a filing system is that each rule was paid for.

Stage by explicit path. Several sessions write in the same repository at the same time. Twice, a session added every changed file to its commit at once, and swept in another session's work: once it destroyed an edit outright, once it pushed half of a colleague's move between two repositories. Nothing was lost the second time, and the record says that was luck, not method. So now a hook refuses the command before it runs. It was tested on twenty forms of the command, and eighteen behaved as written; the two that did not were repaired the same day. The session that created this book's repository met that hook on its very first commit, and was told why, in those words, before it could do any harm.

Read the time from the clock, never compose it. A session writes a time on every message. Sessions, it turns out, invent times: they write a time that feels right after the last one. Nobody notices until a made-up time crosses midnight and a message is filed under the wrong day. When the central session measured itself, five of its twenty-five stamps had been composed, the worst by forty-two minutes, and four of the five were older than the law that forbade them. Across the other desks, thirty-four of a hundred and fifty-one stamps were composed, on thirteen of the seventeen desks measured. The rows behind that figure are published, because the first time it was published the rows had been thrown away and the number could not be defended three hours later. Five weeks after the law, the central session composed a stamp again. Four written warnings had not stopped it; a peer reading a file did. The note it left is the best sentence in the protocol: a reminder is not a mechanism.

Words name states, never people. A session once reported my working tree as "dirty". Work that is not yet committed is not dirty, and very often it contains no error at all; and a word that judges the work judges the one who made it. So the record keeps a table of words the estate does not use, with the word it uses instead.

What no counter can see. The sound plane of the library held six hundred and twenty-two passing assertions across nineteen guards while it was, to any listener, broken. I heard four defects that no counter reported: a voice too quick to understand, a sentence cut before its end. The law that came out of it says that a thing nobody has perceived is in a state, not in failure: unperceived is a state, and the page must say so. That law is why every chapter of this book carries the line "not yet read by the author" until I have read it.

The loop is seconds, not minutes. I stopped two sessions over the same eight-minute test run. It was measured: six seconds of the eight minutes were coverage, the rest were three sweeps that tested nothing new. It was rewritten to twenty seconds. I had written, in my own words, that it "takes a lot of time and should be rethinked". The law was written by a session; the sentence was mine.

Never ask without saying how. A session once asked me to check whether a figure was right, and gave me no way to check it. I answered: please never demand a thing without telling me how to get it. Now every request addressed to a person carries the exact command, the exact path, the exact line to read.

You can see the shape. A failure, dated. A rule, written where the next session will read it. Then, when the rule is broken anyway, a mechanism. Some laws reached the last step, some are still a written rule, and the record says which.

Where the laws touch code, the library itself can hold them. Its house rules are validators that run over a graph of the code, the sixth law of the intelligence architecture made runnable: rules an agent can run before it commits, not folklore it must guess. One of them is about words:

Haro
cCode = "class Shop" + nl + "def KillOrder()" + nl + "  return" + nl
aFindings = StzCheckCode(cCode)
? aFindings[1][:rule]
#--> no-aggressive-verbs
? aFindings[1][:message]
#--> aggressive verb in method 'KillOrder' -- prefer Remove/Delete/Dispose/Clear/Close (Softanza tone)
? StzCodeIsClean(cCode)
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

Read the last line twice. The code is still clean. The tone rule warns; it does not refuse. A word rule advises, and the record says so in its own doctrine: the word law is ruled rather than checked. Here is the remedy the message proposes:

Haro
cCode = "class Shop" + nl + "def RemoveOrder()" + nl + "  return" + nl
? len( StzCheckCode(cCode) )
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

And the rules are a closed set, which an agent can list before it writes:

Haro
? len( StzCodeRuleNames() )
#--> 14
? StzCodeRuleNames()[3]
#--> no-aggressive-verbs

ran: printed what this block promises

That tone rule entered the library in July 2026, five weeks before the estate ruled on its own words. The record does not link the two, so I will not either. But it is the same instinct at two altitudes: the words we use about work are part of the work.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused a framework. The arrangement is files, a history and a few hooks. A supervisor that schedules agents would be one more program to trust, and one more thing that decides without a record. Here, a session that is not running leaves only its files, and the files are the truth.

I refused to let a coordinator grade its legislator. Authority runs down from me; correction runs up from any session to the central one, and from the central one to me. A coordinator that judged its own rules would be the one part of the system nothing could fix.

I refused to automate to the maximum. From the middle of August 2026, sessions were opened by clocks. On 27 August I stopped them. The record keeps my reason as written then: the routines consumed quota without added value. And it keeps the uncomfortable part: that judgement was the only measurement anybody had, because the cost line every session writes at its close carries no token count. The harness does not tell a session what it spent. Of the three hundred and eighty cost lines written so far, one carries a number. [AUTHOR: What did the clocks cost you, in your own words, when you stopped them on 27 August 2026?] Since then, a timer may run a script, never a model; a session starts when a file arrives in a watched folder, or when I start it.

I refused to rule in my absence. A ruling is written in the record only while I am there. When I asked the central session to settle what was pending on my behalf, on 28 September, the five rulings it took that day are marked as taken on my delegation, so that nobody later mistakes them for mine. The decisions at the front of this book are marked the same way.

I refused to let the protocol become a product. The doctrine of the harness is open, and it is never to be sold: its value is in what it refuses. It has also been proved in one place only, one person, one machine, one filesystem, about fifteen sessions. It has no adopter outside this estate.

And I accepted a loss. The code of the last two years was largely written by sessions, and my hand, which was the style, thinned where they wrote. A study of the record measured it: the promise under each line, the house's way of writing an example, stands at nearly a hundred per thousand lines in the short recipes and at seventy-five in my articles, and at under one in the guards the sessions wrote, which assert in another form. The sessions even took the name of my articles for their test files, a name that a model proposed. I accept the implementation code they wrote. I do not accept that the style a programmer or an agent writes with Softanza should be theirs rather than the house's. That is why the law of Part II exists, and why this book is written in my voice, with sessions as researchers and as the court, and why every chapter waits for my reading before it loses the word draft.

5. The court

No guard of the library proves the protocol. Its courts are outside the library, and I name them by what they do: a hook that refuses wholesale staging; a hook that refuses work when the machine has no memory to spare; a check that the hooks installed are the hooks written; an instrument that compares every stamp with its commit and publishes the rows. They are scripts, not Haro, and this book's reader cannot count their assertions, so they are named here and not in the court line below.

The blocks of this chapter stand on the library's guards of its house rules: coderule_narrated proves that a code rule is a rule over the graph, that the house findings come out on a planted fixture in a frozen shape, that the rules number fourteen, and that a definition or a comment is not taken for a call. codegraph_narrated proves the graph beneath them, and coderule_project_narrated runs the rules over the whole library.

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in scale and in independence. Its frameworks run on many machines for many teams; this protocol has been proved at one person, one machine, one filesystem, and nobody outside the estate has tried it. Its doctrine says so in its own words: these are laws that survived one estate.

The field leads in accounting. A paid interface reports the tokens of every call. This estate's cost record was built to report them and could not, so the most important economic decision it took was taken by feeling.

The field leads in tooling for many writers. Branches, merge queues and owners of folders handle concurrency at a scale the estate has not met; here, the answer is a discipline and one hook, and the hook reads the text of a command, so it also refuses a commit message that merely quotes the forbidden form. That cost is known and accepted.

Where I think the record stands apart is in one habit: each law carries the failure that paid for it, and the record publishes its own rate of breaking its own law. The central desk broke the stamp law more often than the estate it measured, and that number is printed beside the estate's.

7. The limit

  • builtthe protocol, its memos and its ledger of rulings; three hooks that refuse wholesale staging and a flooded machine; the instrument that measures composed stamps; the library's fourteen house rules over a code graph
  • designeda watcher that wakes a session when a file arrives, in place of the clocks; a court of style for the code a programmer or an agent writes
  • absenttoken figures in the cost record; any team outside this estate that has tried the protocol; a check of a word in the reader's own language

What is built: the protocol and its files, the dated memos, the ledger of rulings, three hooks that run in every session on this machine, the instrument that measures stamps, and the library's fourteen house rules over its code graph.

What is designed: a watcher that wakes a session when a file arrives, which is the right replacement for the clocks and is not written; a court of style for the code that a programmer or an agent writes with the library, so that the house style is held by a machine and not by a hope.

What is absent: a token figure in the cost record; any team outside this estate that has used the protocol; and a check that a word reads well in the reader's own language, which the word law asks for and nothing performs. The study that read the record named one more limit, and I leave it here in its words: the protocol that makes the record trustworthy also costs energy the product needs, and I should watch the ratio. [AUTHOR: Do you have a reading of the ratio between the work on the protocol and the work on the product? The record holds none.]

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerStage by explicit path, read a file again before you write it, read the time from the clock. Each rule cost someone an edit.
The analystThe record is data you can query, and it publishes its own error rates beside its rules.
The designerA word names a state, never a person. A message is a closed structure a reader scans in one glance, tested on a reader whose first language is not English.
The decision-makerA ruling is written only in your presence. When no figure can answer a question, decide by judgement and write down that it was judgement.
The educatorTeach a rule with the failure that earned it. A rule whose cost you cannot name is a rule you will talk yourself out of at two in the morning.
The agentYou are a worker with a record. You write a memo, a cost line and a conclusion; the hooks refuse what has hurt others; your stamps are compared with your commits. None of it assumes you are careless. All of it assumes you are many.

9. Exercise

Take the last ten messages, notes or log lines in which you wrote a time by hand. For each, find the moment the system recorded on its own: the commit, the time the message was sent, the time the file was saved. Before you look, write down how many of your times you expect to be later than the system's by a minute or more. Then count.

Your count is the finding. I will not give you mine.

The one line still owed

1. The concept, as the field holds it

In our industry, a platform is proven when someone else runs it for real. The home page shows the logos of companies that use it; a case study tells one of them in two pages. A team that believes in its own product uses it for its own work, and a compiler that is serious compiles itself. Engineers who need a scale have one: NASA's readiness levels, later a standard, where the highest level is a system proven in the place it was built for.

These are reasonable tests, and they all point at the same thing: production. What they do not ask is who saw it work, and what that person said.

2. The first principle

The record carries a solution only when it ran on its own engine and a named person said what they saw. [AUTHOR: Is this the chapter's principle in your words, or would you write another sentence?]

3. The Softanza form

This is the last chapter, and it is about something that has not happened. Let me first show you the floor it will stand on, because the floor exists.

A solution is declared before it is built, and the platform that carries it refuses to be deployed before it is built:

Haro
oSol = new stzPlatformProfile("bank")
oSol.DevelopedOn(:Windows)
oSol.WithServer(:backend, :LinuxServer)
oPlatform = StzPlatformQ("bank")
oPlatform.SetProfile(oSol)
try
	oPlatform.Deploy()
catch
	? cCatchError
done
#--> stzPlatform.Deploy: the platform must be Build() before it can be deployed.
? oPlatform.IsDeployed()
#--> 0
oPlatform.Build()
oPlatform.Deploy()
? oPlatform.IsDeployed()
#--> 1

ran: printed what this block promises

Before anything is real, the solution can run on a twin, a copy of the system that holds no reference to reality. Here a file is written into the twin, read back, and is nowhere on the disk:

Haro
oTwin = new stzVirtualFileSystem()
oTwin.CreateFile("orders/today.txt", "3 couscous")
? oTwin.ContentOf("orders/today.txt")
#--> 3 couscous
? oTwin.OriginOf("orders/today.txt")
#--> virtual
? StzEngineFileExists("orders/today.txt")
#--> 0

ran: printed what this block promises

And at the last door, a solution cannot reach production with a fake service bound in it, whoever asks. In chapter 1 you saw the registry refuse; here the delivery itself refuses, with an entitled person at the controls:

Haro
oReg = new stzServiceRegistry("shop")
oReg.BindSandbox(:payments, new stzPaymentsSandbox())
oDel = new stzDelivery("shop")
oDel.AddBackend("api", "linux")
oDel.UseServicesQ(oReg)
oDel.DeployTo(StzDeploymentSiteQ("host1"), "api")
oDel.SetActor(HumanActor("dana"))
oDep = oDel.Deploy(:Production)
? oDep.WasCommitted()
#--> 0
? oDel.Log().EntriesOfLevel(:error)[2][:message]
#--> sandbox-in-production @ shop/payments

ran: printed what this block promises

The person was allowed to deploy. The deployment still did not run, because a payments service that is a sandbox cannot be what a real customer pays through. This is not a question of authority. It is a question of what is true.

So the floor is there: declare, build, rehearse, refuse the fake, commit through a governed actor. Now the absence.

Softanza has been used. I wrote that in chapter 1 and I hold to it, because the study that first read the record wrote the opposite, that no user outside my own projects had been measured, and I corrected it. A bank in Niamey runs an organisation-assessment product I built, installed on its own network under licence, and the installation guide delivered to the bank attests it. A restaurant in Lyon has been building a platform for neighbourhood commerce with me; the record of that project ends on 25 August 2026, with an amendment closed on 4 August and an owner who took part in the first demonstration and ran a day of field tests with two phones. An organisation in Niger has its hub designed. The site lists, project by project, the lesson each one taught and the file of the library that carries it. Part VI of this book tells their stories.

And the site says, in the same page, what those platforms run on today: ordinary stacks. The bank's is a Python application. The restaurant's is a set of web worlds, each a single file. The organisation's hub is not built. Their declarations are being written as Softanza's own, so that moving them onto the Softanza engine is a change of engine and not of plan. The site's own words are exact: it is a step ahead, not a step taken.

So the line the record does not yet carry is this one: the solution ran on Softanza's own engine, and this is what the user said.

What is between here and that line, read from the record and not composed:

  1. A customer's declarations run on the engine instead of the ordinary stack. The declarations are being written; the move is not made.
  2. The language's own runtime runs the library on the customer's system. Today the blocks of this book are run by the runtime of the former host language, version 1.27, and every page says so under its proof line. The bridge runtime that is meant to replace it was reported on 5 October 2026 to pass, on Windows, every assertion the old runtime passes on the library; its pass under Linux is the next step. Haro's charter was ratified on 1 October 2026, and Haro's own stages pass on its own fixtures. Haro does not run the library yet.
  3. The solution writes its guarantee sheet. The vision asks every solution for five rows, one for each system it answers to, technical, social, ecological, economic and cultural, judged as fixtures, with the machine derived from them. No solution has written one.
  4. Live hosts and a real board. The deployment's verification against a real host or a real account is gated by infrastructure. The declared machine boots and judges itself in an emulator; of the four promises its hosted profile makes, the emulator can check three, and the fourth waits for a watchdog on a real board. No customer runs a production workload on it.
  5. A person perceives it, and the record says who. Not a counter. A person, named, with a date and what they said.

The last step is a law of the estate, and it was paid for. The sound plane of the library once held hundreds of passing assertions while it was, to my ear, broken. Since then, a piece of work that reaches a person through a sense must be perceived by a person, and the record must say who perceived it and what they said. And when nobody has, the law says it plainly: unperceived is a state, not a failure. A report may be honest and still be unperceived.

The record already holds the form of the line. In another plane, on 2 October 2026, I listened to a sound the library made and said, in the words written down: "yes it's real drum!!" It is not a solution, and it is not a customer. But it is a person, a date, and a sentence, and it is what the one line will look like.

The record also holds the opposite, honestly. The pictures the library draws were judged by a model, forty-one of them, twenty right, nine wrong, twelve uncertain, and the record says that no human has looked at them yet. The live run of the payments plane with the organisation's test account was postponed, by me, and reported as unperceived. Neither is a failure. Both are owed.

The decision, and what was refused

4. The decision, and what I refused

I refused to be told the projects did not count. The first reading of the record wrote that no user outside my own projects had been measured. It was wrong, and I said so: Softanza has been used in real projects which, while not complete, gave the feedback that shaped its design. The reading was corrected in the record, in place, with the date. What replaced it is smaller and more honest: the users exist and have spoken; they have not yet run on the engine.

I refused a reference without a document. The site counts a project as a reference only when a document proves it, and it quotes no number of countries and no number of developers. A lesson is listed only when a file of the library carries it.

I refused to move a platform by rewriting it. A customer's platform moves to the engine as a change of engine, not of plan. The declarations are written once, as Softanza's own, and the engine beneath them changes. Rewriting would be faster to announce and slower to trust.

I refused my own figure. I have said aloud how far the bridge runtime has come, as a percentage. The study that read the record ruled that the figure should not be printed without the guard that produces it, and I agree. The stage word is "in construction", and the measured rows are the evidence.

I refused an instrument as proof of a perception. A phase whose evidence is entirely a counter is not done when the thing itself is something a person sees or hears. The counter is a result. The person is the verdict.

5. The court

The floor of this chapter stands on three guards. full_scope_model_narrated, the architect's common ground, proves that a solution is modelled first, that a deployment before a build is refused and logged as an error, and that a model cannot perform the deployment. virtual_system_twin_narrated proves that rehearsal touches nothing real, that the plan narrates itself, and that committing is the one door. service_delivery_narrated proves that a production deployment with a fake bound does not run at all, with every reason named, and that the gate opens once the service is real.

The court of this chapter's subject is not a guard. It is a line in the record: who, when, and what they said. That line does not exist yet.

Read from the library's test tree at commit 93d7a39bd on 2026-10-09 02:34 UTC+01:00. The figure is the number of assertions the guard holds, counted in its file; the site shows each one run.

  • full_scope_model_narrated62 assertionsbase/test/system/full_scope_model_narrated.ring
  • virtual_system_twin_narrated48 assertionsbase/test/system/virtual_system_twin_narrated.ring
  • service_delivery_narrated60 assertionsbase/test/system/service_delivery_narrated.ring

6. The field, and where it leads

The field leads in production. Ordinary stacks run real workloads for real users today, including, by the record's own page, the three platforms of this book.

The field leads in live infrastructure. Its tools drive real providers and real hosts every day; Softanza's deployment verifies against a real host only when the infrastructure is there, and rehearses everything else.

The field leads on hardware in the field. Its devices run in shops and clinics; the declared machine boots in an emulator, and its board is not yet in service.

The field leads on speed. The runtime Softanza measured itself against was faster on every row, by a factor between one and two, and the loss was published.

Where I think the record stands apart is in what it will not let itself say. Every reference has a document. Every stage has a word. The rehearsal runs the same engine that ships. A fake cannot ship and a model cannot commit. And a perception is a named, dated, quoted line, which a logo on a home page does not carry.

7. The limit

  • builta declared platform built, then deployed, and refused in the other order; the twin that touches nothing real; the last door that refuses a fake service
  • designedthe runtime that is the language's own, running the library; the guarantee sheet of a solution in five rows; live hosts and a real board
  • absenta customer solution running on the Softanza engine, and a named person's verdict on it

This whole chapter is a limit, so I will be brief.

What is built: the floor. Declare, build, deploy in order; rehearse on a twin; refuse a fake at the last door; commit only through a governed actor.

What is designed: the runtime that is the language's own, running the library; the guarantee sheet of a solution in five rows; the verification on live hosts and on a real board.

What is absent: a customer solution running on the Softanza engine, and a named person's verdict on it. [AUTHOR: Which of the three projects moves to the engine first, and who will be the named person who perceives it?]

8. Six doors

DoorWhat you take from this chapter
The programmerYour code runs today through build, rehearsal and a governed deployment. What you cannot claim yet is that a customer runs it on the engine, and the record will not let you claim it.
The analystAsk for two things before you count a project as proof: a document, and a named verdict.
The designerWhat you design is judged last by a person's sense. A model's opinion of a picture is a result; a person's is the verdict.
The decision-makerRead the stage word before the promise. Today the court is built, and the customer run is absent.
The educatorTeach that unperceived is a state and not a failure. An honest report can ship on it, if it says so.
The agentYou may rehearse a deployment and explain it. You will be refused when you try to perform it, and the refusal will be written down.

9. Exercise

Declare a platform for a project you own, with one server. Before you run anything, write the line you expect under each of three questions: what happens when you ask it to deploy before you build it; what happens when an assistant asks to deploy after the build; what happens when a person does.

Haro
oSol = new stzPlatformProfile("my-project")
oSol.DevelopedOn(:Windows)
oSol.WithServer(:backend, :LinuxServer)
oP = StzPlatformQ("my-project")
oP.SetProfile(oSol)
# your three questions here, each with the line you expect under it

not run: an exercise, written for you to run

Run it. Then write one more line, the one your own project still owes, in the record's form: who perceived it, on what date, and what they said. If nobody has, write "unperceived", and say why. That line is the end of this book, and the beginning of the next one.

Appendix A

The register of innovations

Draft · not yet read by the author

This page has no code to run.

The study of the record read four inventories the library keeps of itself: the narrations with their titles, the design documents, the engine's phase of paradigm engines, and an outside reader's list of rethought concepts. It crossed them, and found forty-six innovations in seven families. This is that register, as the study ruled it on 7 October 2026, with one column of this book's own: the chapter that tells each row.

Read the register as the study reads it, and no better. It is a reading and not a census. A concept with no narration and no design document of its own was not counted. The study's evidence counts files that name the thing in code outside tests and archives, test files, and the engine module where one exists; it counts files that name a thing, and not tests that pass. I have not re-counted any of them. The study also counted how many pages of the site named each innovation; the site has changed since, and I leave that column out.

Of the forty-six, seven are not told in this book: the adverb engine, named variables, the unified find, object history, the intent-based file interface, natural folder navigation, and the invisible and the lookalike. One more, statistics and the linear solver, is told only in part. They are in the register because the record holds them, and in the shade because this book had to choose.

What the register says

The study's reading, which I keep: what the site names is what has a product page, a principle or an area of the Atlas. What it leaves in the dark is what cuts across the areas. Every paradigm of the first family except those with a page, all twelve engines except the polyglot bridge, the pattern languages as a family, the idiom. This book is in part the answer to that: its parts are cut across the areas, and not along them.

The study also reconciled the twelve engines. The macroplan marks the phase done. Eight of the twelve have a source file under their name in the engine; four have none, which are truth, quantifiers, polyglot and polycode, the first two reported done as libraries. On the library's side three engines have no test file at all: adverb, section merging and named variables. Two of the three are rows 16 and 21 above, which this book does not tell, and the third, row 19, it tells as an absence.

What is not measured

No code was run to make the register. The evidence column counts files that name a thing, and the engine's done marks are the macroplan's. Whether an innovation's narration runs once its stale names are repaired was not tested. A row's chapter in the fourth column is the chapter that tells it, and a row that says "named in" is a row the chapter mentions and does not tell.
